title: Real-Factory Credentials From Customs Shipping Records
one_liner: Turn public US import records into supplier-owned reputation credentials and audit-ready reasonable-care dossiers that prove a factory is a real manufacturer.
customer: Small and mid-size US importers of record (Amazon and Shopify brands, furniture, hardware and apparel distributors) re-sourcing to Vietnam, India, Mexico and Turkey. Customs brokers are a channel, and factories are the second payer.
problem: The importer of record is investigated first, and liability turns on whether it exercised reasonable care about the supplier's origin claims. In August 2026 the White House published a report on transshipment, a 40% penalty tariff applies, and CBP has expanded inspections of shipments from Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Mexico. Small importers cannot tell a real factory from a trading company or a re-labeller, and sourcing agents' claims are unverifiable.
solution: Supplier Proof. Build a profile per factory from three or more years of US import records (shipper and consignee names, volumes, product codes, ports, cadence) plus corporate registry and location data, flag anomalies such as volume beyond plausible capacity, mismatched product codes or shell-company addresses, and add optional local inspector visits. Factories claim and verify their profile and can consent to name repeat buyers as references. The output is a dossier the importer can hand to a broker or to CBP.
why_now: Tariff enforcement moved in 2025-26 from headline rates to origin verification, and the August 2026 transshipment report has put importer liability on every compliance officer's desk. Sourcing shifts away from China are happening now, so millions of dollars of orders are going to unfamiliar factories.
revenue_model: Importer subscriptions of $149-499 per month, $150-400 per dossier, inspector visits passed through at a margin, and $600-1,200 per year from factories for a verified credential once importers demand it.
non_obvious_insight: Import records are the only unforgeable cross-border reputation ledger for factories, but they are sold as raw rows to analysts. Repackaged as supplier-owned credentials with a reasonable-care wrapper, a data product becomes a compliance product with a real budget line: avoiding a 40% penalty.
first_30_days: Buy 12 months of import records for two categories (for example furniture and hardware from Vietnam and India). Auto-build about 1,000 factory profiles and hand-audit 20. Send 200 emails to sourcing managers and customs brokers. Sell the first 10 dossiers at $250 each and use them to refine the scoring.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: ImportGenius, Panjiva (S&P Global Market Intelligence), Descartes Datamyne, ImportYeti. White space: The narrow wedge that appears unserved is a fixed-price, human-reviewed 'reasonable-care file' for a small US importer, sold through customs brokers. The SMB importer (Amazon or Shopify brand, or a $2-50M distributor) needs one factory checked before one PO. Enterprise tools (Sayari, Altana, Tradeverifyd, Trademo, Exiger) are sold by demo and are priced and scoped for large compliance teams. Data tools (ImportGenius, Panjiva, Datamyne, ImportYeti) sell rows and leave interpretation to the analyst. Inspectors (QIMA) and sourcing agents (Sourcify) sell physical checks, not a documentary file that maps to CBP's reasonable-care standard. The part I found nobody offering is a factory-claimed profile with consent-based buyer references, which is a two-sided credential. No visible player runs a supplier-owned reputation credential built on customs ledgers. However, the wedge is thin. (1) ImportGenius already markets 'supplier verification via shipping history' at the same $229-449/mo price band. (2) The raw-data floor is free or near-free. (3) Any one of Altana, Trademo or ImportGenius could add a 'transshipment risk report' feature quickly. (4) The factory-pays credential side has no demonstrated demand and needs a two-sided marketplace. Risks I could not check with the exhausted search budget: whether resale of licensed bill-of-lading data is allowed, that US import records often name the forwarder or trading company as shipper instead of the factory, that importers can request confidentiality under 19 CFR 103.31, and that no CBP safe-harbor exists for third-party dossiers.

title: Solar Job Escrow: Bankruptcy-Proof Project Records
one_liner: A neutral escrow that captures every financed solar job's permit, design, serial and step-in authorizations before the installer fails. The installer pays per job, the lender enforces deposits through milestone funding, and cure is paid from the final milestone the lender is still holding.
customer: Payer: mid-size residential installers (300-3,000 loan-financed jobs a year) that need financing access and a trust signal after Freedom Forever. Gatekeeper and co-seller: dealer-risk and credit heads at solar lenders and credit unions (GoodLeap, EverBright, EnFin, Credit Human-type), who can make escrow a dealer-tier condition. Channel: installer CRM, design and project-management platforms that embed the deposit.
problem: When an installer dies, the permits, interconnection applications, PE-stamped designs, serials and portal logins are locked in the dead company's name, and the lender starts from zero. Every other party (lender, homeowner, trustee) finds out after the fact. Before failure, all of that data exists and is easy to copy. After failure it is expensive to reconstruct. The parent product only starts once the loss has occurred, which is why it is lumpy, price-pressured and crowded.
solution: Each job auto-deposits a continuity pack at each milestone: signed contract, permit application and approval, PE-stamped design set, interconnection application number, equipment serials by BOM, and time-stamped site photos. Two pre-signed documents go with it. The homeowner signs a successor-contractor authorization as an addendum at the point of sale, and the installer signs a step-in consent. A written trigger (insolvency, license suspension, or 60 days of no activity) releases the pack to a designated successor. The lender's funding portal requires a complete pack before releasing M1 or M2, so deposits cannot be skipped. Trigger jobs are cured at a pre-agreed per-AHJ rate card. The cure is paid from the last milestone (M3) the lender still holds on that job, plus a small installer holdback. Lenders also get a continuity score per dealer (record completeness, PTO lag, license and lien status). Homeowners get a 'job protected' certificate that installers can use in sales.
why_now: Freedom Forever's collapse made 'will you still be here at PTO?' the first objection at every kitchen table, and made lenders' dealer-risk teams look for controls beyond credit checks. The 25D end is shrinking installer margins and raising failure odds. Agentic capture and CRM APIs make per-job record collection cheap enough for a $60-100 fee. ABS investors can now cite a specific 2026 case when they ask sponsors about continuity.
revenue_model: Installer pays $60-100 per job (about 0.2-0.3% of a $30-35k job). Lender pays a platform fee of $5-10k a month for dealer continuity scoring and pack access. On a trigger, cure work is billed at $1.5-4k per job plus a $500 PTO bonus, funded from the held M3 milestone. Later: a workmanship warranty backed by the reserve, and a recognized 'backup installer' role in ABS structures. Illustration: 3 pilot installers at 800 jobs each is roughly $145-240k a year in deposit fees before lender fees or cure revenue.
non_obvious_insight: The cure budget already exists. On many dealer-channel loans the final milestone (roughly 10-25% of the loan) is not paid until PTO, so on every stranded job the lender is still holding thousands of dollars that would have gone to the dead installer. The only missing piece is a pre-signed right to spend it. And the escrow has an enforcement mechanism that software-escrow lacked: the lender controls the money, so 'no pack, no milestone payment' means installers deposit because that is how they get paid. The party who needs the protection (the lender) is not the party who pays (the installer), and making escrow a sales badge and a dealer-tier perk closes that gap.
first_30_days: Draft the continuity pack spec and the successor-contractor authorization with a solar or construction attorney. Map contractor-of-record change rules for the 10 largest AHJs and top 2-3 utilities in one metro. Recruit 5 installers through former installer ops people and offer a free 90-day pilot in exchange for the badge. Call 3 lender dealer-risk heads with a one-page pitch: escrowed dealers get faster funding or lower holdbacks, and you get a first-call cure vendor. Target 3 installer LOIs and 1 lender pilot letter by day 30, and first live deposits by day 60. Riskiest assumption to test: will a lender change its funding conditions for a pilot dealer group. Test it with a credit union first.
lineage: mutation of I1175 ('Finish Crew: Stranded Solar Job Completion'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: GreenLancer (Solar Repair / O&M network), Lender in-house step-in (GoodLeap, Sunrun, EverBright, EnFin, Credit Human, Participate, Project Solar; also Dividend Finance), Atma Energy (installer taking over stranded Freedom Forever jobs), Local rescue and completion contractors (Revival Solar, ECG Solar, Optimus Energy Solutions, Advance Solar, Solar Discovery). White space: The unserved wedge is portfolio-level, event-driven triage, not crews. (1) Forensic records recovery at scale. No competitor found sells a forensic pack per stranded loan (AHJ permit file, utility interconnection record, dead installer's CRM and design files, distributor and consignment serials, photo audit) sorted into cure tiers with a cost-to-cure and expected-PTO dashboard across a lender's whole book. GreenLancer and the local rescue firms all work job by job. (2) Servicers, credit unions and ABS trustees without operations. The seven Freedom Forever financiers have ops teams, and Sunrun and GoodLeap have crews. Solar Servicing LLC (which took over Mosaic's servicing), credit unions, bank holders and ABS investors have no step-in playbook. I found no completion vendor aimed at them. (3) Legacy stranded books. Titan (an estimated 150,000 households), SunPower, Sunnova, PosiGen, Mosaic-financed loans and others. Lenders may not know which loans sit on de-energized systems, so an identify-then-cure offer has little competition. (4) Standby retainer plus pre-negotiated per-AHJ and per-utility contractor-of-record transfer playbooks for the next failure. Not white space: the first-wave Freedom Forever completion work. The stay-relief order dates to about August 2026, so the seven named financiers have probably already picked contractors, and GreenLancer says it already serves seven financiers. | How this version avoids them: GreenLancer, local rescue contractors and Atma all start after failure, job by job, for an already-staffed lender. This owns the pre-failure moment, sits inside the dealer agreement and the installer's workflow, and earns recurring per-job revenue from installers. When a trigger fires, the company is first-called under a pre-signed rate card and can subcontract to GreenLancer-style shops or local firms. Lender in-house step-in desks have no installer-side records capture, and installers work with 3-5 lenders and will not deposit into five separate lender portals, so neutral multi-lender escrow wins. Solar Insure and OhmSnap serve owners after bankruptcy, and Enphase's program is post-PTO. Main risk is a big lender building a proprietary version, which the neutral multi-lender position is meant to counter.

title: Bedside Coverage Recovery for Safety-Net Hospitals
one_liner: A pay-on-success desk that helps safety-net hospital financial counselors convert lapsed or presumptively covered patients into full Medicaid within the shrinking retroactive window, with informal-income evidence built over text message, paid a flat fee per approved case by the hospital's revenue cycle budget.
customer: Patient financial services and revenue-cycle leaders, plus hospital presumptive eligibility (HPE) and Medicaid enrollment managers, at safety-net, critical-access and county-owned hospitals in expansion states. Start in Nebraska and adjoining expansion states, where the state hospital association has already campaigned against retroactive-coverage cuts. The enrollee pays nothing. The hospital pays only when a case is approved.
problem: Two hospital-side facts changed. First, starting January 1, 2027, retroactive Medicaid coverage for expansion adults shrinks to one month before the application month (per Justice in Aging and other H.R. 1 explainers), so every day a lapsed patient waits to reapply can turn a billable encounter into charity care. Second, HPE screens for the work requirement by attestation and gives up to 60 days of temporary coverage, after which the patient needs a full determination, and hospitals are being urged to build conversion assistance. Projections cited by Applied Policy put FY2027 coverage losses at 2.3M, with about 43% procedural. The hospital sees the loss first: an inactive eligibility response at registration or the ED desk. But the counselor's usual application flow stalls on cash, gig and informal workers, who cannot produce payroll or wage records. The hospital eats the bill. (Assumption to verify: existing hospital Medicaid-eligibility outsourcers handle standard applications but not informal-income compliance evidence.)
solution: A Coverage Recovery Desk delivered as a light workflow, not an EHR integration. (1) Daily feed: a CSV or SFTP list of registrations with inactive or self-pay coverage and prior Medicaid, plus HPE patients at day 20 of 60. (2) Outreach in hours: hospital-branded SMS or WhatsApp in the patient's language. (3) Evidence build: the attestation and receipt engine from the sibling Cure Desk, with third-party attestations for cash workers. Patients who have a bank or payroll trail are routed to the state's own Emmy or SteadyIQ flow. Exemption triage and any state-optional excused months for inpatient stays are documented. (4) Retro-clock calculator: maps each open encounter to the one retroactive month and tells the counselor which filing date protects which claims. This is the hospital-specific feature, and the first thing they will use daily. (5) Counselor submits with a complete packet; we never decide eligibility. (6) Dashboard: dollars of self-pay converted to Medicaid-billable, by lapse reason. Digital-trail patients cost us almost nothing, so margin comes from doing the cash residual efficiently.
why_now: Jan 1, 2027 combines the work requirement, six-month renewals for expansion adults, and the retroactive-coverage cut, all landing on the hospital revenue cycle at once. Uncompensated care is already implicated in rural hospital closures. Hospitals are being told to strengthen HPE-to-full-Medicaid conversion assistance now. Cheap messaging, OCR and translation mean a counselor can handle several times more cases per day than with paper and phone tag.
revenue_model: Pay-on-success, no software fee to start: a flat $150-300 per approved reinstatement or HPE-to-full conversion, tiered by encounter dollars at stake. A flat fee per approval, not a percentage of Medicaid collections, because Medicaid billing-agent payment rules generally restrict percentage-of-collections arrangements (counsel to confirm). Optional $2-4k per month CFO analytics tier (self-pay at risk by lapse reason, retro-window leakage). Illustrative unit economics (assumptions to validate in the audit): a 150-bed hospital sees 120 lapse-related self-pay encounters a month, 25% are reinstated at $200, giving $6k a month or $72k a year per hospital, versus a Medicaid-paid stay worth thousands. 30 hospitals is about $2.2M ARR. Later: subcontract informal-income packets to incumbent eligibility outsourcers.
non_obvious_insight: The hospital registration desk is the earliest reliable detector of work-requirement and procedural terminations, because an eligibility check runs at every visit. Plans learn from monthly files, and states rely on notices that cash workers miss. It is also the moment of maximum patient motivation, with the bill in hand. Plans are limited to a supporting role under the IFR and MCO procurement is slow, but hospitals are neither plans nor determiners, and their counselors already file Medicaid applications every day. The cash-flow logic is lopsided: a $200 fee against a stay Medicaid may pay thousands for, and the one-month retro window makes speed a priced variable for the first time.
first_30_days: Send 15 Nebraska and regional revenue-cycle leaders a free 'lapse leakage audit': they share a de-identified 90-day list of self-pay encounters with prior Medicaid, and we estimate dollars at risk and how many are informal-income cases (procedural lapses today stand in for work-requirement lapses). Sign a BAA and a pay-on-success pilot with the first one or two. Run 20-25 live cases by hand: the counselor works from our SMS templates and packet PDF, and we track time to filing, approvals and the encounters saved by the retro-clock calculator. In parallel, ask the state Medicaid agency and a hospital association contact how reinstatement, reapplication and HPE conversion work for noncompliance terminations, and get counsel's sign-off on the fee structure.
lineage: mutation of I0573 ('Medicaid Hours Wallet for Gig Workers'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: CMS Emmy (Eligibility Made Easy) app and Emmy API, SteadyIQ (Income Passport / Verification Hub), Digital Public Works, Maximus, Optum, Acentra, Deloitte, Gainwell, Conduent, Curam/Merative (state-side community engagement modules). White space: Nobody I found sells an enrollee-side monthly ledger to MCOs or FQHCs that ingests bank, gig and pay-stub data, computes $580 or 80 hours against a state's look-back rules, and produces a state-specific 30-day cure packet. Nothing turned up in searches, CMS vendor pledges or CBPP/KFF/Georgetown landscape coverage. Vendors sit on either side of that gap. State-side vendors (SteadyIQ, Emmy, Maximus, Optum, Deloitte) sell to state agencies. Provider and plan-side vendors (Pointcare, Findhelp, mPulse) sell eligibility monitoring and outreach without gig-income packet building. The clearest unserved segment is workers with no digital trail: cash, informal and 1099-below-threshold workers such as day labor, cleaning and landscaping. Consent-based verification (CBV) via payroll, bank or gig platforms cannot reach them. The 30-day cure step, meaning a compiled packet after a noncompliance notice, is also not addressed by any product I found. The wedge is narrow and could close quickly. States with CBV (SteadyIQ, Emmy) let the enrollee connect accounts directly, which makes a separate packet redundant there. MCOs may be poor buyers because the IFR bars plans from determining compliance and gives them only a supporting role. Pointcare and Findhelp already own the FQHC and MCO relationships and could add a module. Research limits: my web search budget ran out after four searches, so I relied on page fetches. I could not load the CBPP vendor landscape, the Health Affairs piece or the Federal Register text (all blocked), and I could not confirm what Propel for Plans does or any vendor's funding. | How this version avoids them: Pointcare sells lapse detection and retention to FQHCs before claims reject, while this sells recovery and conversion to hospital revenue cycle after lapse, with a different buyer, trigger and pricing. Findhelp sells eligibility-at-risk flags to plans, states and CBOs. mPulse and Propel do outreach and notices. None of them builds informal-income evidence or the retro-clock, and none prices on a hospital's approved case. SteadyIQ, Emmy, and the state-side vendor pledges serve states, and digital-trail patients are handed to them. The cash and informal residue they cannot reach is the only part we do. The buyer is not an MCO, which removes the IFR supporting-role restriction and slow plan procurement. New risk not covered by the parent's research: existing hospital eligibility outsourcers. Mitigate by offering our packet builder as their informal-income subcontractor and by staying on the pay-on-success pricing they already understand.

title: Town-Paid Private Road Census and Formation Bounty
one_liner: Sell New England towns (and their municipal insurance pools) a four-week census of every private road's legal status and emergency-access risk, then earn a per-road bounty for each neighbor group converted into a recorded association with a named point of contact.
customer: Town managers, road commissioners and fire chiefs of small and mid-sized Maine towns (2,000-15,000 residents), then NH and VT. Multi-town buyers: regional councils and planning commissions, and municipal risk pools that fund loss-control services for member towns (Maine Municipal Association's risk program, NH Primex, Vermont VLCT PACIF, all from prior knowledge and unverified here). Secondary payers: developers, via a road-association setup line on the town's subdivision application fee. Residents co-pay a small share.
problem: Every town has dozens to hundreds of private ways with unknown legal status. The town usually cannot spend public money on them (varies by state, to be confirmed per state), yet it is blamed when an ambulance or plow cannot pass a failed culvert, when a subdivision road approved on the condition that a road association be formed decays years later, or when residents petition the town to accept a broken road that would cost six figures to rebuild to town standard. After a storm, state aid wants an organized counterparty. NC's post-Helene private-road program (verified) required a single point of contact and proof of ownership, plus a 50% cost share. The town has no inventory to hand over. Neighbors are stuck in a collective-action deadlock, because nobody wants to be the one who calls the meeting.
solution: Step 1, a fixed-price Private Road Census, roughly $6,500 per town. We ingest parcel GIS, E911 road-name files, registry-of-deeds documents and any culvert or bridge inventory the town has. Language models read the recorded instruments to flag whether a maintenance agreement exists and what it says. For each private way we output parcels served, recorded instrument yes/no, whether an active association exists, contact if any, single-access and stream-crossing flags, and a fire-truck-passability risk score reviewed with the fire chief. The town gets a ranked list, map and memo. Step 2, activation. The town mails a letter on its own letterhead to the top 40 roads with a pre-filled petition for the statutory meeting. In Maine a few owners can petition a notary, and the town letter breaks the who-goes-first deadlock. We run the meetings, and an attorney-supervised covenant is recorded. The town pays a $600 bounty for each completed association (recorded instrument plus officers and point of contact), and residents co-pay about $500. Step 3, a registry subscription at about $2,400 per town per year. It keeps contacts, insurance certificates, reserve attestations and condition photos current, and yields a disaster-ready roads list for the state emergency agency after a storm. Step 4, the town adds a setup fee to subdivision applications so new roads get an association and reserve schedule at approval.
why_now: The cost stack collapsed. Reading recorded instruments for 120 roads used to mean about 120 title searches at hundreds of dollars each. With document extraction plus human QA it is roughly a tenth of that, which is what makes a fixed-price census possible. Storm events keep exposing the same gap, and NC's $175M program (verified) shows states will pay for repair but only through an organized counterparty. Parcel GIS and E911 layers are now open in most New England states. Municipal risk pools are always looking for loss-control programs to justify member subsidies (hypothesis to test). The disaster-aid windows (NC applications closed Feb 2026) show that the next program will again favor roads that are already organized.
revenue_model: Census $6,500 per town, or a regional-council package of 10-12 towns at about $55-65k. Formation bounty $600 per association from the town, plus a $500 resident co-pay, or about $1,100 per road. Registry $2,400 per town per year. Developer setup fee about $1,200 per new subdivision, collected through the town. A town with 120 private ways where 60% are informal has about 70 candidates. If 40% convert in year 1, that is 28 roads, about $31k in bounties and co-pays, plus census and registry, or about $40k per town in year 1. 25 towns would be about $1M. Conversion rate is the key hypothesis. Risk pools could subsidize the census for members, making the insurer a second payer.
non_obvious_insight: The town is not buying road repairs or software. It is buying a legal counterparty for roads it cannot touch, plus a defensible record that it knew about the risk and acted. That is liability hygiene, an easier budget line than subsidizing private roads. The official letter is the cheapest neighbor-activation channel that exists, because it dissolves the who-goes-first deadlock that makes formation so slow closing-by-closing. One buyer delivers dozens of roads, which inverts the parent's per-road CAC. The census data, once assembled across towns, becomes a state-level inventory that emergency agencies, lenders and title underwriters would pay for.
first_30_days: Pick one pilot town with open parcel GIS and online registry access, ideally a lakes-region Maine town of about 4,000 people. Build a free 30-road slice of the census in 10 days from public data. Walk it to the road commissioner, fire chief and town manager, and ask them for the 5 roads they fear most. Ask to mail an official letter to 10 pilot roads and run 2 statutory meetings within 30 days. In parallel, call 3 regional councils and the risk-management teams of the Maine, NH and Vermont municipal associations to test whether they would subsidize census work as loss control. Target one signed $4,500 first-town census (typically under small-purchase thresholds, to be confirmed) and one pilot association recorded. Riskiest assumptions: town willingness to pay a per-road bounty, and letter-to-meeting conversion above 25%.
lineage: mutation of I0048 ('Private Road Associations in a Box'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: PayHOA, Mainstream HOA and community-association platforms (Buildium, AppFolio, FrontSteps, Vantaca, CINC and similar), DIY legal templates and local real estate attorneys (Nolo, US Legal Forms, LegalZoom-style forms, local attorney drafting), Public alternatives: state road-association statutes and county road or special-assessment districts. 1. No product I could find bundles the closing-triggered legal package (state-specific maintenance agreement, county recording, a lightweight entity) with the ongoing administration for informal neighbor groups. PayHOA covers dues admin generically and cheaply; the statutes and the law-firm and forms market cover formation; nobody stitches them together for the 5-60 home private road.

We create the association, and dues admin stays a thin link to whatever tool the road picks. DIY templates and local attorneys: they serve a single closing, and we are town-sponsored and mass-produced with attorney supervision behind it, so we are a customer of their legal review rather than a rival. State statutes and county road districts: we operationalize the statute at scale for towns rather than asking residents to self-serve. NC Private Road and Bridge Program: a demand proof and a template for who will need our pre-qualified registry after the next storm. Local road-association managers (unidentified): potential subcontractors for annual administration, not competitors for a town-level census. Town asset-management and GIS vendors such as Cartegraph or OpenGov (from prior knowledge, unverified): they track public roads and would not create legal counterparties on private ones.

title: Daubert-Ready Sample Audits for Litigation Surveys
one_liner: A neutral data-quality auditor that gives survey experts and litigators a signed, control-calibrated audit of the respondent sample behind a Lanham Act, false-advertising or damages survey, or a teardown of the other side's sample.
customer: Wedge: the 30-60 US testifying survey experts and boutique survey-litigation consultancies who field likelihood-of-confusion, secondary-meaning, deception and conjoint-damages surveys, plus the IP and false-advertising litigation partners who retain them. Later: in-house counsel at CPG and pharma companies that run claim-substantiation surveys for FTC or NAD challenges.
problem: A litigation survey is only worth what survives cross-examination and a Rule 702 challenge. Until recently 'we removed speeders and failed attention checks' was an adequate answer on sample quality. Agents now pass those checks (99.8% of 6,000 trials in the parent's evidence), so the standard defence is hollow. Opposing experts can attack the panel, and the amended Rule 702 (Dec 2023) makes the proponent show reliability by a preponderance. Survey experts have no neutral way to show their sample is clean, and rebuttal experts have no fast, credible way to quantify contamination in the other side's produced respondent data. The fee is small next to the $50k-$300k+ a litigation survey costs (from background knowledge, to be verified in calls) and the case value behind it.
solution: Two case-driven products. (1) Proponent audit: before full fielding, insert canary and honeypot items (with the expert's sign-off) and run a pilot. Ingest detection signals licensed from dtect, Verisoul or DQC rather than building an ensemble. Field the test and control cells on a 150-300-complete slice of a licensed address-recruited panel (NORC, Ipsos or Verasight-style, resold, not built). Deliver contamination-adjusted net-effect estimates with bounds, a sensitivity table ('conclusion holds up to X% contamination') and a hash-timestamped chain-of-custody field log. A named academic methodologist signs a declaration that can be attached to the expert report. (2) Rebuttal teardown: a fixed-scope 10-business-day analysis of the opposing side's produced respondent-level data, built to fit rebuttal-report deadlines. The firm never opines on the merits (confusion, deception, damages). It only certifies or attacks data quality, so it is a supplier to every expert rather than a competitor.
why_now: Agents that pass attention checks (2025-26) killed the old defence. Pew's Aug 2026 finding of 18% bogus respondents in opt-in samples, with trap questions and Sentry disagreeing on who is bogus, gives opposing counsel a citable, public source. The Dec 2023 Rule 702 amendment gives judges an explicit mandate to scrutinise reliability. The first contested Daubert motion where an expert cannot rebut agent contamination will spread fast through the small survey-expert community.
revenue_model: $12-40k per case engagement (proponent audit or rebuttal teardown), billed to the law firm as consulting-expert cost and passed through to the client. $60-120k/yr retainers for survey-expert firms that run 8-15 surveys a year, covering unlimited pilots and field-log stamps. $2-5k per survey for a hash-stamped field log as a low-touch add-on. Later, a $25-50k/yr library subscription for in-house claim-substantiation teams. Gross margin is mostly the licensed control slice (about $3-8k per engagement) plus methodologist hours.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is not paying for truth. The buyer is paying, with the client's litigation budget, for insurance against cross-examination, so willingness to pay is set by case value and not by the $/complete price that caps every other idea in this space. The test-versus-control design used in litigation surveys also means random-answering bots hit both cells and pull net confusion toward zero. Contamination therefore tends to hurt plaintiffs and help defendants, so both sides have a reason to buy: proponents to insulate, opponents to attack. Once a court admits or credits the method, it becomes citable precedent. That is process power and switching cost that no detection API can copy.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: list every survey expert named in published Lanham Act opinions of the last five years and 40 IP litigation partners. Run 10 price-validation calls (5 experts, 5 partners) and stop if fewer than 4 say $15k+ is reasonable. Days 10-25: buy about 300 completes each from 4 panel vendors on a classic Eveready-format and Teflon-format design, plus a 150-complete control slice from a licensed address-recruited panel. Measure how many bots it takes to swing net confusion by 5 points. Days 20-30: publish 'How many agents does it take to flip a confusion survey?' as a white paper and CLE talk proposal. competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Data Quality Co-op (DQC), Verasight, Verisoul, CloudResearch (Sentry, Engage, Bot Olympics). White space: Detection is crowded and getting cheap: Verisoul, Roundtable, dtect, CloudResearch, Kantar Qubed, Research Defender, PureScore, ReDem and CleanID all sell it, some at cents per respondent. Cross-supplier scorecards already exist too, since Data Quality Co-op is a neutral clearinghouse. Building a detection ensemble or a generic vendor scorecard would be a fifth-to-tenth entrant against funded players.

What I did not find anyone selling:
1. A per-study ground-truth calibration. This means running a slice of the same questionnaire on a verified, address-recruited human control group and then reporting contamination-adjusted estimates with error bounds. Every vendor I found detects and removes. None quantifies how much bias survives the cleaning, and none re-estimates the result against a known-real reference. Pew's finding that voter-file matching removed valid respondents and made the error worse suggests 'remove the flagged' is itself a source of bias.
2. A neutral buyer-side referee that owns no sample. dtect is neutral but only sells entry-time detection. DQC is neutral but does not audit individual studies or supply a control sample. Verasight owns verified humans but sells sample.
3. Independent, third-party verification of the vendors' own accuracy claims. CloudResearch and Verisoul each claim 100% agent detection from internal or self-run tests. The Bot Olympics is MIT-judged but tests CloudResearch's own system.

The missing piece for a startup is the control panel. Building an address-recruited, device-attested panel of about 2,000 people is slow and expensive. The likelier route is to partner with or license an existing one (Verasight, NORC, Pew or Ipsos-style panels), not recruit from scratch.

This conclusion has limits. My WebSearch budget ran out at 200 calls, so I could not run the Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt checks or search for a second wave of small startups. I also could not confirm funding for DQC, Roundtable, dtect or Verasight. | How this version avoids them: Detection vendors (Verisoul, dtect, Roundtable, CloudResearch, ReDem, CleanID) sell entry-time filtering to panels at cents per complete and produce nothing a court can use. They are input suppliers here. Data Quality Co-op's scorecard and Data Trust Score describe suppliers in general and do not give a case-specific, testifiable declaration. Verasight owns verified humans but sells sample, so opposing counsel would call it conflicted. Pew and NORC publish the methodology for free but not per case, and not in expert-report form. Panel-owner stacks (Kantar Qubed, Research Defender, PureScore, Pori) are the self-grading problem that Daubert challenges target. Existing litigation-survey consultancies field surveys and testify on merits, so they are customers, not rivals.

title: AltSchool Without Buildings: Disability Programs in Host Schools
one_liner: AltSchool burned $170M+ building its own schools; in Texas, the new voucher money can only reach accredited schools with two years of history, so rent that eligibility by running clinician-led disability programs inside half-empty accredited private schools.
customer: Payer: Texas families with children on IEPs holding Texas Education Freedom Accounts (about $10k standard, up to $30k for IEP students at accredited private schools). Partner: small accredited private schools, often church schools, with empty classrooms. Supply: speech-language pathologists, BCBAs and dyslexia therapists who want to run a program.
problem: TEFA rules require private schools to be accredited and to have operated two consecutive school years, and microschool or learning-pod students get only $2,000. Families holding $30k accounts cannot find seats with real special-ed capacity. Eligible incumbents have buildings but no special-ed expertise. Clinicians have expertise but no eligibility.
solution: An operating company signs a host agreement with an accredited school. The school enrolls the students as school of record and receives the TEFA funds. We supply a clinical director, staff, structured-literacy or ABA-informed curriculum, IEP compliance, the annual norm-referenced testing TEFA requires for grades 3-12, and ESA billing reconciliation. Start with 8-10 student cohorts (dyslexia and autism support). Confirm with each host's accreditor that a program-within-a-school structure is acceptable.
why_now: TEFA's first year is starting (2026-27): $1B in funding, more than 130,000 applications in the first three weeks, roughly 100,000 families expected. Texas public schools lost about 76,000 students this year and are closing dozens of campuses. Federal special-ed enforcement was hollowed out (OSEP layoffs in October 2025, with the office reportedly moving to HHS in June 2026), so parents are looking for alternatives.
revenue_model: Management fee of about 20-25% of ESA revenue per student ($6-7.5k per $30k student, so $60-75k per 10-student program per year), with a 15-20% host share; one-time program-design fee ($3-5k) per host; compliance and reconciliation SaaS later.
non_obvious_insight: AltSchool's mistake was building schools. In Texas the moat is accreditation plus a two-year operating history, which are other people's assets, so partner instead of build. Empty church-school classrooms, underemployed clinicians and $30k accounts form a three-way arbitrage that only exists because of the new rules.
first_30_days: List about 150 small accredited private schools in DFW, Houston, San Antonio and Austin using accreditor directories. Send heads of school a one-page economics sheet. Recruit 10 clinicians via LinkedIn and SLP/BCBA Facebook groups. Sign 1-2 pilot hosts for a January 2027 cohort and collect pre-enrollment interest from TEFA parent groups. First revenue is host design fees, with per-student revenue starting once enrollments transfer.

Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Fusion Academy (Nord Anglia), Brightmont Academy, Prenda (microschool platform), KaiPod Learning. White space: Research caveat: the WebSearch budget (200 calls) was exhausted before any searches ran, so this verdict rests on about 30 direct page fetches, not the planned 6-12 searches. Google-style discovery of funded startups was not possible, and the negative finding below is unproven. Crunchbase (403), the Comptroller TEFA program pages (404), TEPSAC (503) and several news sites failed.

What the fetches found: no direct competitor was located that runs clinician-led disability programs inside host accredited private schools as the school-of-record structure and bills against TEFA. Adjacent players cover each piece separately.
- Learning-differences schools that build their own campuses: Fusion, Brightmont, Rawson Saunders, Fairhill.
- Microschool platforms: Prenda, KaiPod, Primer.
- Clinician marketplaces: Presence.
- Outside operators embedded in private schools: Catapult.

The unserved wedge is the three-way structure itself. It is a management company that supplies the clinical director, staff, IEP compliance, norm-referenced testing and ESA reconciliation inside a host school. It targets IEP families holding up to $30k accounts in metro Texas in the first TEFA year.

Three risks decide whether the white space is real, and none is resolved:
1. **Legality and accreditor acceptance.** Statute text says a private school must be accredited by a TEPSAC-recognized organization and have continuously operated a campus for at least two school years. It does not address programs within a school or microschools. If the Comptroller, TEA or the accreditor treats a hosted program as a separate campus, or as renting accreditation, the model fails. A 100% pass-through of the ESA to the host with a 20-25% management fee could also draw scrutiny.
2. **Incumbents and hosts.** Existing specialist schools already have eligibility and expertise and may simply expand. Host schools take on IEP compliance liability and reputational risk.
3. **Unit economics.** A 10-student cohort at 20-25% yields $60-75k a year, before clinician cost. Whether that covers a BCBA or dyslexia therapist plus a clinical director was not tested.

title: Contingency Hunters for Unbilled Water Revenue
one_liner: Find the 'ghost parcels' and slow big meters that leak revenue out of a utility, using assessor rolls, building footprints, imagery and billing data, and get paid 20-30% of what is recovered so the city risks nothing.
customer: City, county and district water and sewer utilities with 10k-200k connections. The buyer is the finance director or utility director who is facing a council fight over the next rate increase.
problem: Utilities are raising rates 5-10% a year to fund PFAS treatment, lead line replacement and aging pipes, and councils are pushing back on affordability. Meanwhile revenue leaks out in places nobody owns: structures with no water account (unpermitted ADUs on shared meters, converted garages, fire and irrigation taps never billed), commercial compound meters that are 20-30 years old and under-register at low flows, meters swapped without the account being updated, stopped or zero-read accounts that never get investigated, and sewer-only accounts billed off a bad water read. The customer information system, the GIS parcel layer and the assessor roll sit in different departments. Nobody owns the join, and nobody has staff to do it.
solution: Join the utility's account list and consumption history to the assessor roll (building sq ft, units, use code), permits, open building-footprint datasets and aerial imagery (pools, irrigated area, added structures). Build an expected-consumption model by parcel. Rank the mismatches: no account at all, consumption far below expected, sudden step-downs after a meter change, and large meters whose low-flow profile looks wrong. A small field crew and a meter-test partner verify the top leads. The utility gets a documented recovery list with legal-ready evidence, back-billing calculations that respect the state's limits, and a meter-replacement plan. The firm takes 20-30% of first-year recovered incremental revenue.
why_now: Rate shock and affordability politics in 2025-26 make 'recover what we're owed before raising rates' an easy story for council. Open building-footprint datasets and cheap vision AI make expected-consumption modeling accessible to a two-person team, and utilities that finished smart-meter rollouts now have interval data that has never been analyzed for revenue. Contingency work also clears procurement easily because there is no upfront cost.
revenue_model: Contingency of 20-30% on the first 12-24 months of recovered annualized revenue, plus a fixed fee for a meter-testing and replacement plan. Later, a recurring SaaS monitor ($1-3 per 100 accounts per month). Optional referral fees from meter and test vendors.
non_obvious_insight: The leak that matters is not in the pipe. Large commercial meters are about 10-20% of accounts but 40-60% of revenue, and the oldest ones quietly under-register the low flows that hospitals, hotels and factories use all night. The utility never sees this loss because the meter is the thing measuring it.
first_30_days: Pick a county whose assessor roll and building footprints are downloadable and whose utility publishes or will release account addresses (public-records request). Run a free scan and generate 20 named addresses with expected versus billed usage. Cold-email finance directors at five utilities with 'we'll show you 20 unbilled addresses before you sign anything'. Sign the first contingency contract with a city that has a rate hearing scheduled, and verify leads with a hired meter-testing subcontractor.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Itron (Temetra Analysis / Non-Revenue Water portfolio), Badger Meter (BEACON, OneNetwork), Master Meter (Harmony Encore MDM), Metron-Farnier (WaterScope). White space: Important caveat: my WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) before any of my searches ran. This verdict rests on about 20 direct page fetches and GitHub repo searches, not on broad web, Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt sweeps. Treat 'no direct competitor found' as unconfirmed, and do a manual pass on Crunchbase, YC and RFP portals before committing. What I did verify: (1) I found no vendor selling a contingency-fee service that joins assessor roll, footprints, imagery and the billing system to produce named unbilled addresses for water utilities. (2) The metering and analytics incumbents (Itron, Badger, Master Meter, Metron) sell software tied to their own hardware, with no evidence of a ranked, dollar-denominated, legal-ready recovery list or contingency pricing. (3) The GitHub search for open-source tools found nothing relevant. Unverified, from background knowledge: engineering and rate consultancies (Raftelis, FCS, Hazen and similar) do apparent-loss audits and revenue-protection reviews on a fee basis. Contract meter-testing firms and meter distributors run large-meter testing and right-sizing programs, usually to sell replacement meters. Small local billing-audit shops may exist. Genuinely unserved: an independent, outcome-priced screen of large-account meter accuracy that ranks specific accounts by expected dollars using consumption history, and that does not depend on one meter vendor's hardware. Ghost-parcel discovery is the weaker half. A structure with no account is rare where permits trigger taps, and an ADU on a shared meter is usually already billed on consumption. Back-billing is politically and legally messy, and some jurisdictions restrict contingency contracts. The larger risk is structural (yield, procurement law, optics), not competitive.

title: Delay-Risk Underwriting Desk for Data Center Insurers
one_liner: Sell Delay-in-Start-Up underwriters a 5-day hall-level readiness review and a portfolio 'collision calendar' so scarce DSU capacity can be written on more projects with fewer surprises, funded by the insured through a policy subjectivity, and later share in the premium.
customer: Delay-in-Start-Up underwriters and engineering leads at construction and specialty carriers and Lloyd's syndicates, plus the construction-broker teams that place data center DSU, and reinsurers. The insured (sponsor or lender-as-loss-payee) funds the work through a policy subjectivity. Later: backstop providers whose payout depends on delay thresholds, for example a backstop that only triggers if construction is under about 180 days late.
problem: DSU is the most contentious and expensive element of data center construction cover. Zurich commentary says adding it cuts available capacity, and underwriters call it disproportionate to premium. A flood of AI data center submissions is hampering underwriters' ability to process them, and DSU capacity is being reserved for projects judged best risk-managed. Delay exposure can exceed $1B on a single campus. Carriers now require phased handovers and detailed commissioning protocols, and they ask who is building, what equipment is specified and how commissioning sequences, but they can only check documents. DSU claims later need programme evidence, commissioning records and contemporaneous project records that are rarely captured cleanly. Worst, DSU losses are correlated through shared scarce pools (OEM startup crews, CDU and coolant-chemistry lots, utility energization windows) that per-risk underwriting cannot see.
solution: Four layers, sold in order. (1) Pre-bind 'DSU Readiness Review' in 5 business days per submission: desk review of the commissioning plan and sequence, capacity check of the contractor and OEM startup technicians, the utility energization path, a stage-appropriate Readiness Ladder score, and an underwriter-facing recommendation on deductible, waiting period and warranty wording. The underwriter commissions it and makes it a bind subjectivity, so the insured pays. (2) In-policy monthly Ladder monitoring, framed as compliance with the commissioning-protocol warranty, with early warnings to the underwriter. It also builds the contemporaneous evidence file for any delay notice, which cuts adjusting cost and disputes. (3) Portfolio 'Collision Calendar' for carriers and reinsurers: how many insured halls need the same OEM startup crew or utility window in the same month, so accumulation is priced rather than discovered. (4) Year 2: delegated authority. We become an MGA or coverholder on DSU excess layers, or offer a readiness-triggered parametric top-up where a verified Ladder milestone missed by a date is the trigger, earning a profit commission.
why_now: Insurers began rationing DSU exactly as data center project sizes jumped, with average project value rising from roughly $150M to roughly $3M+ per the coverage above. Aon expanded its Data Center Lifecycle Insurance Program to $2.5B in January 2026, covering construction all risks, DSU and operational damage/BI. Brokers publicly call DSU the pressure point. GPU-backed lenders and offtakers increasingly want delay cover as a condition of their deals, which pulls more submissions into an already constrained market. Document AI now turns commissioning scripts, test reports and punch lists into structured evidence for cents per page, so a small bench can serve many risks.
revenue_model: $12-25K per pre-bind review, paid by the insured through the subjectivity. $4-8K per month per policy for monitoring. $75-200K per year for carrier and reinsurer portfolio analytics. From year 2, a 10-20% profit commission on DSU premium written under delegated authority, which creates outcome-linked economics: we earn more when our screening keeps loss ratios low. Bottom-up: 40 reviewed risks and 25 monitored halls in year 1 is about $0.8-1.2M, before any delegated-authority income.
non_obvious_insight: Underwriters do not buy diligence, they buy capacity. A credible hall-level score lets a carrier say yes to more DSU premium at the same loss ratio, so the buyer has a revenue reason to pay rather than a cost to minimize. Second, the pre-bind, in-policy and claims evidence needs are the same ledger, so one dataset serves three insurer budgets (underwriting, risk engineering, claims). Third, and most non-obvious, DSU is a systemic-correlation business disguised as a per-project one. Ten independently insured halls that all need the same OEM's startup crew in the same month are one risk, not ten. Nobody has the hall-level calendar to see it, and reinsurers will pay to.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 Cx leads plus one former DSU underwriter or claims adjuster as a paid adviser. Build a loss-cause taxonomy of about 6 delay causes from public litigation, insurer and broker commentary on delayed data center projects. Map about 20 DSU underwriters and construction-broker teams. Offer 8 of them a free shadow review, delivered in 5 days on a live submission with details blinded. Aim for 2 shadow reviews completed and 1 paid pilot by day 45. Insurance cycles are slow, so accept that. Riskiest assumption to test first: carriers will make an outside readiness review a subjectivity instead of relying on in-house or outsourced risk-engineering surveys. Ask each underwriter directly how surveys are commissioned today and who pays.

title: Record-on-Request Desk for Superior Courts
one_liner: A managed compliance service that lets a superior court answer any indigent litigant's request for a verbatim record with one certified record per request, priced per record delivered and using the cheapest lawful method, whether steno or electronic recording.
customer: Court executive officers and presiding family/probate judges of small and mid-size California superior courts, especially those outside the AB 3013 pilot or above its 10-20% cap. Self-represented litigants and DV legal aid are the users, but the court is the payer.
problem: FVAP v. Superior Court (Aug 10, 2026) gives indigent litigants a mandatory right to an official verbatim record on request, through court-paid pro tem reporters or electronic recording. Courts have no reporters and hiring freezes, and they cannot staff for requests that could arrive any day. Their real gap is a defensible request-to-record workflow: intake, indigency check, method selection, delivery of a certified appeal-ready record, and reporting. The 3 million hearings without a record are already a Judicial Council-visible metric. Half-day pro tem minimums make each request cost $450-500 or more.
solution: A per-request desk, priced by outcome. The litigant or facilitator files a request when they set the hearing, so the desk usually gets 2-7 days of notice, which turns random demand into schedulable demand. The desk picks the method: (a) the court's own recording plus a certified transcript on demand (subcontracted to an eScribers-style vendor), or (b) a physically present steno reporter from a pooled roster that covers several requests in the same courthouse (the offspring-1 network) when a steno record is required or the department has no recording. The court pays only for records delivered and certified. A dashboard shows requests, turnaround and no-record rate by department, ready for Judicial Council reporting. The desk is offered at no retainer with a quarterly spend cap, sized to the court's own budget.
why_now: The Supreme Court decision is Aug 2026 and the court decision names the compliance routes, so every court now needs a plan, and no incumbent has packaged one. Reporter budgets and vacancy savings exist because courts cannot fill positions, and CA has already sent dedicated funding to court reporters (verify the current allocation and whether vacancy savings can be redirected). Verbit's Judicial Council master agreement for captioning from July 1, 2026 shows courts do buy court-tech through master agreements, which gives a path from single-court pilots to statewide.
revenue_model: The court pays a flat $150-250 per hearing record delivered (up to 30 minutes), certified transcripts at a per-page rate, and no retainer. Pricing sits below a $450-500 half-day pro tem and far below an idle full-time reporter. Steno requests use pooled reporters, and audio requests use subcontracted transcription, so gross margin is about 30-40%. Year 2: annual subscription for the dashboard and intake software, and a statewide master-agreement bid. Legal aid and foundations can fund 'request navigators' who file requests for litigants, which lifts volume.
non_obvious_insight: The court does not need reporters. It needs a defensible answer to a request, so the method is irrelevant, and the biggest threat (electronic recording) becomes a supply input to a desk that will choose it. Requests that arrive at intake instead of at the courtroom door are what make pooled steno economical, because notice converts unpredictable demand into a schedule. Outcome pricing ('pay only when a certified record is delivered') is the contingency that lets a risk-averse court say yes without a retainer.
first_30_days: Week 1: one-week legal check with a court-reporter licensing attorney, plus reading the ruling's list of lawful compliance routes. Weeks 1-3: ask FVAP and 2-3 DV legal-aid groups to introduce court executives of two counties with the highest no-record rates. Build the intake form and an eScribers-style subcontract, and sign 3 physical pro tem reporters in one county. Weeks 3-4: offer one family department a no-cost, at-cost 60-day compliance pilot (about 20-40 requests) with a weekly report. Aim for an under-threshold purchase order or sole-source urgent-compliance pilot within 90-120 days. The 30-day success test is a signed pilot letter from one court and a design-partner agreement with FVAP.
lineage: mutation of I0248 ('Fifteen-Minute Court Reporting for Family Law Hearings'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context: Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Steno (Steno Agency Inc.), DirectDep, StenoScout, Incumbent agencies (Veritext, Esquire, Combs Reporting, Coalition Court Reporters). Code 69959 says 'Remote court reporting shall not be used by courts to make the record of any court proceedings' and defines it as a stenographer not present in the courtroom (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959/). The only exception, Gov. Code 69959.5, allows remote reporting only by 'full-time official reporters ... employed by the participating superior court', physically in a court facility, in 13 pilot counties, capped at 10-20% of reporters (https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/government-code/gov-sect-69959-5/). title: A Price Reporting Agency for Trade Materials
one_liner: Turn pooled supply-house invoices into contract-grade, SKU-level price evidence for the trades, starting with cost-change certificates that win price-adjustment change orders and ending as the index that escalation clauses and price-lock guarantees reference.
customer: First: plumbing, HVAC and electrical subcontractors with $3-30M revenue that carry fixed-price bids, multi-month jobs and maintenance agreements and eat cost changes between bid and buy. End state: the counterparties who write and argue escalation clauses, meaning general contractors, property owners and managers, municipal procurement, insurers, home-warranty programs, lenders, and the manufacturers and distributors who want realized-price data.
problem: Price adjustment requests are argued with anecdotes. A sub says copper fittings and water heaters are up 15-20% since the bid, and the GC or owner asks for proof. Broad public benchmarks (producer price indices and estimating books) are category-level and lag what contractors actually pay by SKU at their contractor multiplier in their region, and supplier price letters flow to contractors with a long lag, as the parent's tariff research noted (50% Section 232 copper duty from August 1, 2025). Subs either absorb the difference on fixed-price work or lose weeks assembling invoices by hand. There is no independent, contract-grade reference that both sides of a contract accept, as far as the parent's research and I could find. Parent idea limit: a per-shop audit keeps price data private and never becomes anything a counterparty trusts.
solution: Step 1 (months 0-6) sells a Cost-Change Certificate. For a sub with a fixed-price contract or bid, we parse its own supplier invoices and quotes into a SKU-normalized evidence pack: cost at the bid date versus cost at purchase, supplier price-letter references, invoice copies, and the escalation amount calculated by the contract's own formula, reviewed by the shop's accountant. It needs no network on day one, only one shop's invoices. Step 2: every certificate is paid partly in data, since the shop opts in to contribute its anonymized line items to the pool and in exchange gets a free alert feed ('your PEX-A fitting cost is 9% above the regional median'). Step 3 (months 6-18): publish weekly transaction-based indices by category and region, with a 30-day lag, minimum-contributor thresholds, no supplier or shop names, to stay clear of price-signaling and confidentiality problems. Owners, GCs and municipalities start writing 'adjusted per [Index] Copper Fittings, Region' into contracts and pay for verified access. Step 4 (months 18-36): price-lock guarantees for quoted jobs, underwritten off the index through an MGA or reinsurer partner, where shops pay a small premium on covered materials and we carry the basis risk we understand better than anyone.
why_now: Tariff-driven cost swings made price adjustment a routine dispute in 2025-26, and owners and GCs are rewriting price-adjustment language. The barrier to a transaction index was always normalizing hundreds of supplier catalog and invoice formats into comparable SKUs, and LLMs just made that cheap. Field-service and accounting systems make invoice ingestion easy. The volatility also means the certificate solves a painful, dated, dollar-denominated problem today, not a theoretical data project.
revenue_model: Certificates at $250-400 each, or 15-20% of the escalation actually approved (better alignment on big claims). Then index subscriptions of $500-2,000 per month for GCs, owners, insurers and municipal buyers who want verified reference access, with data licensing to manufacturers and distributors for realized-price and sell-through data. Later underwriting margin on price-lock guarantees, priced at roughly 1.5-3% of covered materials. Example: a sub with a $400K contract that is 30% materials and 8% higher-cost has a $9,600 claim, and a 20% success fee on half of that approved is about $1,000 per contract.
non_obvious_insight: In commodity markets the durable business is not the data feed but being the named reference in contracts, which is why price reporting agencies for metals and lumber have switching costs no feed provider has. The way in is not a dashboard. It is a document that ends an argument, sold to the party who is losing money now. The certificate requires no network on day one, and the network appears as a byproduct because every certificate adds contributed data. It is also a position platform vendors and supply houses structurally cannot take. ServiceTitan and Kojo depend on supplier integrations such as Ferguson and Hajoca, and publishing cross-customer price data pits those partners against their users, while a supply house cannot publish its own multipliers.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 light-commercial mechanical and plumbing subs with open fixed-price contracts where costs have risen since bid (owner peer groups, PHCC and ACCA chapters). Build the SKU normalizer for the top 200 SKUs (copper tube and fittings, PEX, PVC, water heaters, gas flex) across Ferguson, Hajoca, Winsupply, Home Depot Pro and local-house formats. Produce 5 certificates within 2 weeks and record how each GC or owner responds, since approval rate and dollars approved are the key learning. Sign 3 shops to the contingency version. Publish a free monthly 'copper fittings' note from the first shops' data (with disclosure) to seed the brand. Have an attorney review the contribution agreement and the aggregation and lag rules before publishing anything pooled. Web search was unavailable to the parent researcher, so verify that no existing indices or claim-documentation vendors serve this niche.

title: Failed-Part Bounty for Insurance Subrogation
one_liner: Pay plumbers a bounty to bag, photograph and chain-of-custody the pipe, supply line or fitting that failed, then sell the evidence and a brand-level failure database to insurers' subrogation units and manufacturers.
customer: Subrogation departments and subro vendors at regional and mutual homeowners insurers (the ones too small to send a forensic engineer to a $9k supply-line loss). Second buyers: plumbing manufacturers, distributors and private-label buyers who license the failure data.
problem: Water damage is among the top two homeowner claim categories. Product-defect subrogation (a supply line, PEX fitting, toilet connector, ice-maker line or water heater that failed early) only works if someone kept the failed part. The plumber is on scene 1 to 3 days before the adjuster, cuts the failed piece out, and tosses it in the truck-bed scrap bin. When the adjuster arrives the evidence is gone, the insurer eats the loss, and the manufacturer's lawyers cite spoliation. Insurers only hire the $2,000 forensic engineer on the big losses, so the routine $8-15k losses are never pursued. Meanwhile every plumber knows which brands are failing (certain plastic-nut braided lines, certain fill valves, certain fitting lots) but nobody aggregates it.
solution: A 90-second protocol and kit. Tamper-evident bag with a QR label, a phone flow (photo of the part in place, photo after removal, the manufacturer stamp or date code, homeowner e-signature by text, and the claim number if one exists). A weekly courier pickup from the shop and a climate-controlled evidence locker. Optional one-page factual cause-of-loss statement drawn from the same photos (sudden burst versus long-term seepage, which is exactly the 'gradual leak' exclusion that decides whether homeowners get paid). Every part is logged by brand, model, date code and failure mode, which builds a Backblaze-style public failure-rate report by product line. Insurers get the part plus a ready evidence package. The shop gets a bounty and a small line item on the invoice.
why_now: Water-loss severity has risen sharply and carriers are under pressure on homeowners loss ratios, so they are hunting for recovery dollars. Copper and steel tariffs plus the shift to PEX and imported fittings have flooded the market with cheaper components of unknown quality. Photo and OCR tooling now makes a cheap, standardized evidence workflow possible, and the subrogation trade press is openly saying evidence preservation is the make-or-break step.
revenue_model: Insurer or subro vendor pays $75-150 per part with a documented chain of custody, of which $40-60 goes to the shop and tech. Plus a 3-8% success share on any recovery that follows. Plus annual data licenses ($15-60k) to manufacturers, distributors and big-box private-label buyers, and per-report fees for expert-witness-ready packages.
non_obvious_insight: The evidence that decides tens of millions in recoveries is currently destroyed daily by the only people who touch it first, and the reason is not malice. Nobody pays a tech to spend 4 minutes and a bag on a piece of scrap. The plumber, not the adjuster, is the true first-notice-of-loss for the product itself. The bounty is a price signal, and the dataset that falls out is one nobody else can buy.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 shops through a local PHCC chapter and the owner Facebook and peer groups with a flat $50 per bag and a free kit. Design the label and the phone flow in a form tool. Collect the first 50 parts with photos. Take the first 20 case files to two regional mutual insurers and a subrogation vendor and ask them which they would have pursued. Sell a paid pilot for 100 parts on the strength of their answers.

Insurer-funded plumber networks exist (LeakBot). Plumber field software exists (ServiceTitan, CompanyCam). title: Implant Payment Index for ASC Networks
one_liner: Pool invoice-versus-payment data across physician-owned ASC networks to build the payer-by-procedure benchmark that only payers hold today, and turn it into the reference price index that carve-out contracts cite instead of each ASC's own invoice.
customer: First buyers are ASC management companies, physician-owned ASC networks of 5-40 centers, and state ASC associations, all facing payer contract renewals. Later buyers are ASC developers, lenders and PE sponsors building pro formas, and eventually payers licensing the index.
problem: Every carve-out claim hands the payer the vendor invoice, so payers hold the largest SKU-level implant price database in the country and use it in contract talks. Becker's July 2026 reported that this year's payer talks came down to fine print, implant costs and case-level cost data. ASCs' invoices are trapped in AP, so each ASC negotiates knowing only its own numbers. Drugs have a public ASP benchmark, while devices have none, so carve-outs reference each ASC's invoice. Payers distrust that (invoice inflation, related-party distributors) and demand attachments, which creates the paperwork and the leak in the parent idea.
solution: Wedge product: the Payer Implant Scorecard. From de-identified 835s, case lists and a sample of invoices, per payer and CPT it reports the share of implant lines paid $0, realized payment as a ratio of invoice cost, markup actually realized versus the clause, and how the network's terms compare with peer networks. It ends in a negotiation memo with the dollar impact of each ask. Data is contributed give-to-get, and contributors also get a free carve-out lookback that feeds the recovery business. Governance: cells need at least 5 contributors, data lags at least 90 days, nothing is forward-looking, and outputs are ratios rather than vendor prices, with antitrust counsel reviewing the protocol. Then a quarterly published Implant Reference Index and a Model Carve-Out Clause (index plus X%, no per-claim invoice attachment). Later modules include developer and lender pro formas by payer mix and, eventually, a payer license.
why_now: Implant cost is the central ASC economics story of 2026 (Becker's, March and July 2026). Volume is moving to ASCs as CMS's CY2026 rule reportedly expands the ASC covered list; verify the exact list. Payers are using AI payment-integrity tools that will only get stricter on attachments, which gives them a reason to want an index. Invoice and contract extraction is cheap enough to build the dataset without armies of coders.
revenue_model: Networks pay $25-60k a year, or about $2-4k a facility a month, for the scorecard and quarterly refresh, plus a success fee of 10% of the first 24 months of measured implant reimbursement uplift after a renegotiation, measured on the same 835s. Data and pro forma licenses to developers, lenders and sponsors are later. A payer index license comes only once the index is a contract reference. Bottom-up: about 1,000-1,200 implant-heavy physician-owned ASCs at roughly $30k a year is $30-36M before the index and lender products.
non_obvious_insight: The information asymmetry runs in the opposite direction from what ASCs assume. Payers already hold the invoices, since ASCs have been sending them for years, but ASCs do not hold each other's. Because the deliverable is a ratio (paid divided by invoice cost) and not a price, it can be shared without breaching vendor price-confidentiality clauses. Once contracts reference the index, both sides drop the per-claim attachment process that causes the leak. A neutral index is also something an ASC-billing company or PM vendor cannot publish, since it would expose their own clients' leaks and their customers' data-sharing limits.
first_30_days: Recruit 3 ASC networks or MSOs plus one state ASC association, preferring those with payer renewals in the next 6 months. Week 1: offer a free 'zero-pay scan' that needs only 835s and a case list, showing the share of implant lines (L8699, 027x, C-codes) paid $0 by payer and CPT. Week 2: engage antitrust and health-privacy counsel to sign off on the data protocol and BAA/de-identification. Week 3: for the first network, add 20-30 invoices per top payer and CPT to convert zero-pay rates into dollars. Week 4: deliver the first Scorecard and negotiation memo for a live renewal, and sell a paid $15-25k pilot to two more networks. Kill signal: no network will pool data even under the protocol, or scan results show payers already pay implants at cost-plus almost everywhere.

title: Replication Bench: Poll-Triaged Experiments With Signed Records
one_liner: A poll-first replication service: anonymous postdoc consensus tells biotech investors and AI-bio builders which claim to test, and a pool of laid-off bench scientists runs the decisive experiment and returns a signed, machine-readable execution record.
customer: Seed and Series A biotech VCs, corporate venture arms and pharma BD teams evaluating spinouts (poll memos and replications). AI-first biotechs and AI-for-science startups with agent swarms and no wet lab (ticketed experiments). Later, licensees of the replication registry.
problem: Investors can buy candid consensus but can't cheaply convert it into a test. Agent-driven startups can buy experiments, but cannot tell which literature claims their designs are built on. A bench network alone has speculative, nascent demand from agents. A poll shop alone has no way to run the decisive experiment.
solution: Bench Pulse: within 5 business days, 8-15 vetted, paid, anonymous subfield postdocs and senior techs give a structured memo on the named claim (consensus, red flags, fragile reagents, what to test first). Where the poll narrows the question, the same team runs 'Key-Figure Replication' at rented bench space with pre-registered success criteria. Each job returns a signed record separating protocol, human edits and physical execution (deviations, photos, instrument logs, raw data). AI-agent customers order the same protocols through an API and can request 'claim-verified' runs before building on a paper.
why_now: There is a large pool of laid-off molecular biologists and postdocs available at near-market rates, seed funds are scrutinizing academic-spinout claims harder, and AI-for-science startups are producing agent-designed experiments faster than anyone can run them.
revenue_model: $4-6k per poll memo, $15-40k per key-experiment replication, $30-60k per year fund retainers for pipeline-wide bench pulse, $1.5-8k per agent experiment at roughly 35-45% gross margin, and later licenses of the labeled replication registry to AI-bio firms.
non_obvious_insight: Poll consensus is the cheap triage that decides where a $15-40k replication is most informative, so the bench network needs less capacity to make more money per experiment. Each replication then scores the poll: 'polls predicted X of Y outcomes' becomes proof that lets the company sell poll-only memos at scale. Every job adds to a labeled dataset of what replicated, what didn't and why, in a machine-readable format, which is precisely what AI-for-science companies lack and can't obtain from papers.
first_30_days: Pick one subfield where you personally know about 20 contacts (for example CAR-T, organoids or targeted protein degradation) and draft the NDA and anonymity protocol (about $3k in legal). Recruit 10 laid-off molecular biologists, sublet 2-3 surplus benches, and define a fixed-price ticket type for replication. Offer 3 seed funds a free poll on an asset they are already reviewing, convert one to a paid $5k poll, and upsell a replication. Pitch 10 AI protein-design startups on the same bench.
lineage: hybrid of I0400 + I0868 (Bench-Truth Diligence for Biotech Investors + Human Bench Network for AI Agents). Why stronger: Each parent has a missing half: bench-truth diligence lacks capacity to run the decisive experiment, and the human bench network lacks a buyer with an urgent budget and a filtered question. Together, a $5k poll funds triage, a $15-40k replication uses the bench, and the labeled replication registry becomes a moat that neither Hoeford-style polls nor cloud labs can build.
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Hoeford Research, Alacrita, Fios Genomics, GLG. White space: Caveat on coverage: the WebSearch quota was exhausted (200 of 200) before this task started. I substituted direct WebFetch of competitor pages, Google News RSS, and some Brave and Bing queries. Brave rate-limited me (429) and Bing returned junk. Hoeford and Fios pages were blocked or truncated. So 'nothing found' is weaker than a full sweep, and the founder should confirm with Crunchbase and LinkedIn plus 10 calls to seed VCs.

What I found. Both halves of the idea have adjacent players, but I found no one selling the specific product as described.

Poll half. Expert networks (GLG, Guidepoint, Third Bridge) and scientific-diligence boutiques (Alacrita, Fios) all sell expert input to investors. They interview senior experts and KOLs, sell bespoke projects, and market to finance clients. I found no fixed-price, 5-day, named-claim consensus poll of 8-15 anonymous junior bench scientists. That is a real wedge, and it fits the founder's critique that the incumbents rely on conflicted seniors.

Replication half. 'Wet diligence' at CROs or independent labs is an accepted practice (LifeSciVC says it should be 'gating before investing'). Hoeford appears to sell it. Science Exchange has the marketplace and the history (Reproducibility Initiative, RP:CB). The bundle, where the poll narrows the question and then a pre-registered, blinded replication follows, looks unserved. Owning a bench pool of laid-off scientists is the least defensible and most operationally risky part.

Segment. AI-bio founders building on published wet-lab claims are the least served, but Adaptyv Bio (raised $40M, 3-week assays from $149 per protein) is already serving protein-design validation.

Structural threats.
- GLG or Guidepoint can copy the poll cheaply once it is proven, since they already sell surveys.
- Anonymity is leaky in subfields of 20-50 people.
- Postdocs risk their careers and may breach university confidentiality or employment terms.
- A negative poll about a named PI's paper carries defamation and tortious-interference exposure.
- A replication that fails in a new lab does not prove the claim is false, which is the ambiguity buyers hate. || Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Adaptyv Bio (Adaptyv Biosystems), Ginkgo Bioworks (Cloud Lab and Datapoints), Emerald Cloud Lab, Science Exchange and Scientist.com (CRO marketplaces). White space: Things I did not find. I could not run WebSearch (the session budget of 200 was used up), so this comes from Google News RSS queries and direct page fetches. I did not check Crunchbase, YC's directory, Product Hunt or GitHub in depth; a GitHub repository search returned nothing.

1. No funded company sells human-executed, ad hoc, arbitrary-protocol wet-lab work through an agent-native ticket API with a fixed price and a signed record separating AI proposal, human edit and physical execution. The nearest pieces are split across companies. Adaptyv has the agent API but runs standardized automated assays. CRO marketplaces have custom human work but run on quotes and SOWs. Transfyr has the execution-record capture but no labor. Emerald and Ginkgo have flexible automation but were not found to offer human-run ad hoc work to agents.

That means multi-step, protocol-specific molecular biology that a robot cannot be programmed for in time: novel enzyme or nuclease activity validation, cloning plus cell-free expression plus a custom activity readout, and unusual cell-culture assays. Anthropic's post confirms this is where a frontier lab keeps human scientists.
