The window is narrow and closing.
- Adaptyv has $40M, agent-native positioning, a stated plan to add 'more complex biological workflows', and Chai and Boltz as customers. It can move toward the ad hoc tail with automation.
- Scientist.com and Science Exchange could add an agent API or MCP layer around their existing providers with modest effort.
- Transfyr could bundle records with any CRO.
- Anthropic and other frontier labs are insourcing bench capacity.

Risks to the idea's own claims:
- BioSpace headlines show layoffs are easing: August 2026 biopharma layoffs were about 500, down 90% year over year, and the Q2 job report says postings are rising. Skilled hands are still available, but the 'layoff wave' supply story is weakening (via https://news.google.com/rss/search?q=biotech+layoffs+2026+BioSpace+job+cuts+tracker).

title: Supplier Divorce Protection: Tool Census and Overrun Forensics
one_liner: When a US manufacturer leaves a Chinese contract manufacturer, we find out which molds and dies it really owns, and prove whether the ex-supplier is still running them off the books.
customer: US OEMs and PE-owned manufacturers ($50M-$500M revenue) that moved or are moving injection-molded, die-cast, stamped or extruded product out of China within the last 24 months, and hold $200k-$5M of tooling there. The buyer is the COO or VP Supply Chain, with General Counsel as co-signer. General counsel and brand-protection managers are the second buyer.
problem: Most small and mid-size OEMs cannot say which tools they own, where they physically sit, or what condition they are in. The paper trail is a PO line item from 2016 and a WeChat thread. When the relationship ends, the supplier slow-walks tool release, demands storage or release fees, and sometimes runs overruns on your tooling on a third shift and sells them to distributors and marketplaces at a discount. You then compete against your own product, and lawyers cannot help because nobody can prove which tool made which part.
solution: Three stacked products. (1) Tool Census: a local partner audits each supplier on video and in person, laser-tags every tool with a serial, records its condition and appraised value, and captures a macro-photo 'fingerprint' library of each cavity (gate vestige, ejector-pin witness marks, texture flaws, parting-line signature). (2) Overrun Watch: monitor Amazon, Alibaba, 1688, Temu, eBay and Walmart Marketplace for look-alike parts, buy samples, and match them to cavity fingerprints, date wheels and lot codes with computer-vision-assisted forensics. That yields evidence packs for marketplace takedowns, CBP IPR recordation, or counsel. (3) Tool Extraction: negotiate release, handle Chinese export paperwork and freight, and re-qualify the tool in Ohio.
why_now: The Reshoring Initiative's 2026 survey shows 36% of OEMs reshored this year, up from 29%. The 2025 tariff whiplash ended a lot of Chinese supplier relationships, and the Feb 2026 Supreme Court IEEPA ruling is now churning sourcing decisions again, so the number of messy breakups is at a peak. Cheap macro-imaging and vision models make tool-mark matching, previously an expensive forensic-lab exercise, feasible at SMB prices.
revenue_model: Tool Census at $6k-$15k per supplier site. Overrun Watch at $2k-$5k per month per product family. Forensic evidence pack at $3k-$8k per case. Extraction at 8-12% of appraised tool value plus pass-through freight. Expected first-year ACV per client is $40k-$120k.
non_obvious_insight: Outsiders think IP loss in China means someone copies your design. Insiders know the far bigger leak is your own paid-for tool running unrecorded shifts, and that every cavity is a physical fingerprint the supplier cannot deny. Ownership of the tooling is the real leverage in any break-up, and almost nobody documents it until the day they need it.
first_30_days: Skip China operations at first. Sell a remote $2,500 'Marketplace Overrun Audit': buy 10 units of the client's product from 1688, Alibaba and Temu, compare them to the golden sample and lot codes, and deliver a one-page verdict. Sign 3 design partners through Ohio plant-manager and Reshoring Initiative networks, and line up a Dongguan or Ningbo audit contractor by referral. Book a one-hour consult with an IP litigator who will white-label the evidence-pack format.

title: Cavity ID: Tool-of-Origin Evidence via Counsel
one_liner: Expert-grade 'which tool made this part, and when' reports, built from parts the brand already holds in the US and sold through China-facing IP law firms to brands whose ex-supplier is selling their product.
customer: Wedge: branded hard-goods companies ($10M-$150M revenue: housewares, pet, fitness, hand tools, juvenile, small appliances) that sell injection-molded or die-cast products on Amazon/Walmart/Target, hold a design patent, trade dress or registered mark on the part, and ended a China supplier in the last 18 months. Buyer of record is their outside China/IP counsel (15-25 boutique cross-border firms), who engage us as a consulting expert so the work is privileged. The brand's GC or COO signs off on the disbursement.
problem: The brand sees look-alike units of its own product on Amazon, Temu and 1688 at 30% below its price, and suspects the ex-supplier is running its steel on a third shift. Today its lawyers can send a cease-and-desist built on suspicion, and the supplier answers 'that is a copy, not ours'. Marketplace takedown vendors produce screenshots and listings, not proof of which tool made the part or that it was made after the orders stopped. Without that proof the brand loses the negotiation over tool release, and losing it costs six or seven figures in tooling and margin.
solution: One product, the Tool-of-Origin Report, with no China operations and no extraction business. (1) Baseline: macro-image 30-60 retained parts per SKU, taken from the brand's own US inventory, returns and QA samples across different lots and dates. Build a cavity signature library (cavity ID marks, gate vestige, ejector-pin witness marks, parting-line and texture flaws) plus a wear-over-time curve, since tool wear is monotonic and dates the tool's state. (2) Attribution: test-buy 5-10 suspect units, match them to a cavity and tool state, and report a forensic-style likelihood ratio, including whether the tool state postdates the last PO. (3) Counsel-ready pack: chain of custody, methodology and a signed declaration from a retained independent molding-process engineer, formatted for the Amazon Report-a-Violation and APEX flows, the Alibaba IP platform, CBP recordation, a demand letter or litigation. Monitoring is bought or white-labeled from an existing vendor. Field capture in China is subcontracted, and only in a later pre-exit 'baseline while the supplier is still cooperative' tier.
why_now: The 2025 tariff whiplash and the Feb 2026 IEEPA ruling (per the parent research) have produced a wave of supplier breakups. Formal-entry bulk imports rose after the end of the US de minimis exemption in 2025, which makes overrun sellers easier to reach through CBP and marketplaces. Cheap macro-imaging plus modern vision models make tool-mark statistics feasible at SMB prices, where a forensic lab used to cost $30k+ per case.
revenue_model: Baseline $4,500 per product family. Test-buy attribution report $6,500 per case (up to 10 samples). Expert declaration or testimony $350/hr through counsel. Optional 'Overrun Watch' retainer $1,500/month per family, with two attributions a year included and monitoring white-labeled. Counsel buys the report as a disbursement and marks it up under its own billing, so there are no referral fees, which avoids fee-sharing ethics problems. Target 60 clients at about $14k blended annual spend, roughly $0.85M ARR, by month 12. Gross margin about 65% (assumption). Bottom-up reachable market is roughly 1,500 qualifying brands (assumption to validate).
non_obvious_insight: The evidence a lawyer needs is not 'this is a copy'. It is 'this was made on your steel after you stopped ordering'. Tool wear is a clock: edges round, texture erodes, flash grows, and repairs leave dated marks. So parts you already own in a US warehouse from 2022, 2024 and 2025 reconstruct the wear timeline without ever visiting China. Routing the work through counsel also makes it privileged, and it moves the spend from a marketing or brand-protection budget to a legal-dispute budget that is bigger and less price-sensitive.
first_30_days: Weeks 1-2: interview 12 China-facing IP lawyers and 8 GCs, asking what evidence they wish they had at the demand-letter stage and whether they would buy at $6.5k. In parallel, run a blind validation. Buy multi-cavity molded parts from known sources across 2-3 tool states and test whether our imaging plus statistics assigns cavity and tool state correctly (target above 95%). Publish the methodology memo. Retain one independent molding-process engineer as expert of record. Weeks 3-4: sell 3 paid $2,500 Overrun Audits (test-buys plus a one-page verdict), qualified on the client owning enforceable IP on the part, through one law-firm co-marketing partner. Kill signal: fewer than 3 of 12 lawyers say they would buy, or blind accuracy below 90%.

title: Supervised-Hours Bench for Counselors and Social Workers
one_liner: A managed group-supervision network and hour-logging platform that lets clinics fund the thousands of post-degree supervised hours gating counseling, MFT and social-work licenses.
customer: Group therapy practices, community mental-health agencies and school districts hiring associate-level counselors and social workers; the associates themselves.

Licensure typically requires 2-4k supervised hours after the degree, and associates often pay $50-150 an hour out of pocket for supervision that is scarce and tracked on paper. Clinics cannot hire associates faster than supervisors can be found.
solution: Certified supervisors, often semi-retired licensed clinicians, deliver state-compliant group supervision by video. The platform logs hours in board-ready format and enforces state ratios and rules. Clinics pay per associate per month to onboard associates who can bill insurance under supervision.
why_now: The July 2026 loan caps squeeze students in excluded fields and push them toward employer support. Behavioral-health demand is high, and telesupervision is widely permitted in many states after the pandemic.
revenue_model: $150-300 per associate per month from the clinic, supervision delivery margin, and hour-logging SaaS. Optional share of billed associate revenue.
non_obvious_insight: The scarcest input in the credential chain is not the degree but post-degree supervision, and the payer is the employer, not the student, because associates bill insurance and become revenue-positive once supervised.
first_30_days: Pick one large state that permits telesupervision. Recruit 5 licensed supervisors. Sign 3 group practices with about 10 associates in total. Run the hour logs in spreadsheets first and charge $200 per associate per month. Verify board rules before selling.

title: Contingency Recovery for Contaminated Survey Sample
one_liner: A freight-audit-style recovery firm that finds contaminated and duplicated completes in the survey sample buyers already paid for, files credit claims against panel vendors, and keeps 25-35% of what it recovers.
customer: Wedge: mid-size full-service market research agencies (about 100-500 staff) that buy $1-10M a year of third-party online sample on fixed-fee client projects and absorb the reruns. Second wave: procurement teams at CPG, pharma and financial-services firms that already run recovery audits on freight, telecom and cloud spend but have never applied one to research sample.
problem: The parent idea asks insights teams to pay for a quality audit, and the research found no evidence anyone will pay $3-15k for one. Buyers do pay for money back. Kantar says post-field reconciliation (rejected sample) rates are up about 300% in three years, with some clients rejecting up to 40% of data (a vendor source). Contaminated completes that pass screening are paid for and used. The same panelist or device is also resold through several exchanges, so buyers pay twice for one human. Agencies eat the rerun cost, procurement never sees data quality, and nobody has respondent-level evidence strong enough to make a vendor pay. Vendors also fight individual rejections because their detector disagrees with the buyer's.
solution: Zero-upfront retrospective audit. The buyer gives read access to 12-24 months of respondent-level files, vendor IDs, invoices and MSAs. The firm runs LLM-assisted open-end forensics, cross-vendor duplicate detection (hashed device, IP and open-end similarity) and paradata review. It ingests detection flags from dtect, Verisoul or DQC where the buyer already has them. A 300-500-complete verified-human control cell per major vendor calibrates a population-level contamination estimate with error bounds. The firm then files claims for replacement completes, credits or refunds, citing the contractual quality clause. Claims argue that a vendor's batch exceeded the SLA (e.g. above 5% invalid, 95% CI) rather than fighting each flagged complete, which is where vendors dispute. Fee is 25-35% of value recovered, with no recovery meaning no fee. Stage two is prospective: a payment-hold or escrow layer where vendor payment for a batch releases after a control-calibrated pass, and a monitoring subscription.
why_now: Agents passing attention checks mean the largest share of contamination is now undetected at entry, which is exactly the paid-for-but-invalid pool that recovery targets. The cost stack collapsed: reading 10 million open-ended answers used to need human coders at dollars per complete, and LLMs now do it at fractions of a cent, so a contingency model works even on mid-size invoices. Pew's Aug 2026 study and NORC's fraud review give claim letters a public, credible methodology to cite. Buyers are already 'auditing suppliers, bringing sampling in-house and demanding accountability' (Greenbook), so procurement is primed.
revenue_model: Contingency fee of 25-35% of recovered value. Illustrative unit economics, which are assumptions to test: $3M annual sample spend, 5-10% recoverable ($150-300k), 50% recovered, 30% fee, so $22-45k per customer per year. That is lower than the parent's $50-150k programmes but has almost no sales friction. Add-ons are a prospective monitoring subscription ($2-4k/month) and escrow at 1-2% of sample spend. Roughly 150-250 agencies and 30-60 enterprise buyers as a bottom-up serviceable market gives a $10M+ ARR business without ever selling 'quality' as a line item.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody budgets for data quality, but everyone has a process for accounts receivable. Turning 'is my sample clean?' into 'how much money are we owed?' moves the buyer from the insights head, who has no budget and no pain, to finance and procurement, who have both. The scarce asset is the same verified-human reference as in the parent, but used differently. It is needed only in small doses (a few hundred humans per vendor), which removes the 2,000-person panel problem and lets it be licensed instead of built. Population-level SLA claims also sidestep the detector-disagreement fight that makes per-complete rejections so contentious.
first_30_days: Days 1-7: post to insights and procurement communities and DM 20 agency founders and heads of ops. The offer is 'send one vendor's last quarter of respondent files, we tell you the recoverable amount, you pay nothing unless we recover'. Days 5-15: have a contract lawyer review 10 sample sample-vendor MSAs and SOWs to extract quality, replacement and dispute clauses, and draft a standard claim letter. Days 10-25: build the pipeline (open-end similarity, hashed-device dedupe across vendors, control-cell comparison) and buy 300 completes each from 4 major vendors as baseline. Days 20-30: sign 3 contingency agreements and file the first claim. Success is the first $50k recovered by day 90. Kill if, after 5 audits, recoverable value is below 2% of spend or vendors refuse every claim.
lineage: mutation of I0716 ('Independent Referee for Survey Panel Data'), type: new-customer-or-model
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Data Quality Co-op (DQC), Verasight, Verisoul, CloudResearch (Sentry, Engage, Bot Olympics). White space: Detection is crowded and getting cheap: Verisoul, Roundtable, dtect, CloudResearch, Kantar Qubed, Research Defender, PureScore, ReDem and CleanID all sell it, some at cents per respondent. Cross-supplier scorecards already exist too, since Data Quality Co-op is a neutral clearinghouse. Building a detection ensemble or a generic vendor scorecard would be a fifth-to-tenth entrant against funded players.

What I did not find anyone selling:
1. A per-study ground-truth calibration. This means running a slice of the same questionnaire on a verified, address-recruited human control group and then reporting contamination-adjusted estimates with error bounds. Every vendor I found detects and removes. None quantifies how much bias survives the cleaning, and none re-estimates the result against a known-real reference. Pew's finding that voter-file matching removed valid respondents and made the error worse suggests 'remove the flagged' is itself a source of bias.
2. A neutral buyer-side referee that owns no sample. dtect is neutral but only sells entry-time detection. DQC is neutral but does not audit individual studies or supply a control sample. Verasight owns verified humans but sells sample.
3. Independent, third-party verification of the vendors' own accuracy claims. CloudResearch and Verisoul each claim 100% agent detection from internal or self-run tests. The Bot Olympics is MIT-judged but tests CloudResearch's own system.

The missing piece for a startup is the control panel. Building an address-recruited, device-attested panel of about 2,000 people is slow and expensive. The likelier route is to partner with or license an existing one (Verasight, NORC, Pew or Ipsos-style panels), not recruit from scratch.

This conclusion has limits. My WebSearch budget ran out at 200 calls, so I could not run the Crunchbase, YC or Product Hunt checks or search for a second wave of small startups. I also could not confirm funding for DQC, Roundtable, dtect or Verasight. | How this version avoids them: Detection and scorecard vendors sell information or prevention: Verisoul, dtect, Roundtable, CloudResearch Sentry, ReDem and CleanID filter at entry, and DQC sells supplier benchmarks and a trust score. None recovers money already paid, and all are cheap enough to be input suppliers rather than rivals. Panel-owner stacks (Kantar Qubed, Research Defender, PureScore, Pori) are the counterparty being claimed against, not a competitor. Verasight sells sample and could not credibly run claims against other vendors. The firm takes no referral fees from any vendor and never sells sample, so it stays neutral. Pew and NORC publish methodology free but never file claims. Traditional recovery-audit firms (freight, telecom, healthcare billing) do not touch survey sample, and the defensibility comes from the vendor-by-vendor claim-outcome database, which sets settlement rates and improves each claim.

title: Lab-Sourced Smoke Contamination Benchmark and Loss Index
one_liner: A give-to-get data cooperative that captures post-fire dust wipe, tape lift and air results directly from accredited labs, whoever ordered them. It returns percentile benchmarks to hygienists and adjusters for free, and sells the resulting contamination-prevalence and remediation-cost index to reinsurers, cat modelers, rating agencies and reserving actuaries.
customer: Payers: catastrophe and reserving actuaries at wildfire-exposed carriers, the California FAIR Plan, reinsurance brokers' analytics teams and cat-model vendors, and rating agencies. Contributors, who get the service free: IH firms, public adjusters and 2-3 AIHA-accredited environmental labs. Free-licensed users: DTSC, CDI and LA County, so the index becomes the citable reference.
problem: AB 1795 turns smoke on a standing home into a presumed covered loss with a 30-day clock, yet nobody knows contamination prevalence by distance, home age, construction, HVAC or plume. The only public dataset is EFRU's roughly 50-80 homes (63% elevated lead, one third asbestos, post-remediation). Carrier-vendor data sits in privileged silos. Cat models are built around destroyed structures, and I did not verify whether any vendor has a smoke-on-standing-homes module. Reinsurance and reserving for 2027 must price a blind tail: 13,000+ standing smoke-damage homes in LA alone, with ALE running until clearance. Every hygienist also argues about the comparison basis (urban background dust versus thresholds), and Purdue reports consultants using wrong comparators. No one has a defensible background distribution.
solution: The chokepoint is labs, not reports. Every sample, carrier-side or policyholder-side, runs through a handful of accredited labs. The co-op gives labs a differentiator: a structured electronic data deliverable plus a consent checkbox on the chain-of-custody form ('de-identified results may be contributed to the benchmark'). Contributors get a free percentile report, for example 'kitchen floor wipe lead at the 92nd percentile of 1,400 homes 0.5-1 mile from the perimeter, built 1950-79', plus a neighborhood background-dust distribution that answers the comparator fight. Buyers get a parcel-level contamination probability by contaminant, and an expected remediation-scope and cost distribution calibrated on consenting claims. Delivery is by API, CSV and annual studies, versioned, with a free license to state agencies. Public data (Cal Fire DINS, assessor year built, DTSC soil results) fills the gaps. The model generalizes to CO, OR, HI and any WUI fire.
why_now: The signing of AB 1795 on 9/15/2026 converted smoke from an adjuster judgment into a legislated, presumed, time-boxed loss. Reinsurance and carrier reserving for 2027 must now price the distribution. State standards are two to three years away and the regulators will borrow the largest population dataset available. Labs are commodity businesses hungry for differentiation, and structured data plus LLM tooling makes lab-level ingestion cheap for a small team.
revenue_model: Subscriptions of $40k-$120k a year per reinsurer, cat modeler or carrier. Bespoke reserving studies at $75k-$150k. A data-processing fee of $15-$25 per sample, paid by labs or contributors, for the percentile reports. A later licensing revenue share with cat-model vendors. Balance-sheet option once the index is trusted: a parametric smoke-remediation trigger calibrated on the co-op's data, built with a licensed MGA and reinsurer capacity. That is a 2029 step and needs admitted-carrier or surplus-lines structuring.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone assumes data comes from adjudicated claims and reports. Labs are the only neutral point that sees both carrier-side and policyholder-side samples, and the percentile report solves the hygienist's biggest weakness, defending the comparison basis, so contributors have a selfish reason to opt in. The hard problem is selection bias: policyholder-side samples skew dirty, and carrier vendors sample thinly and shallowly. The co-op only earns trust if it corrects for who ordered the sample, ideally with at least one carrier's vendor data, or with a randomized sampling frame in one neighborhood. Solving that bias is the scientific moat, and it is exactly what a regulator or actuary will test first.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: pitch 3 accredited labs handling fire-zone samples on a consent-based structured feed, aiming for one signed LOI. Request EFRU's dataset and Purdue's reviewed reports under a data-sharing MOU. Days 10-20: assemble the public layer (DINS perimeters and damage inspections, assessor year built, DTSC soil data, CDI task-force figures) and publish a free 'Eaton Fire Smoke Background Dust Benchmark v0' from the EFRU sample (n of roughly 50-100) to seed usage. Days 20-30: sell two paid $15k-$25k 'Smoke Reserving Briefs' to a carrier cat or reserving team and a reinsurance-broker analytics team ahead of renewals. Sign 5 IH firms as contributors. Kill test: if no actuary will pay for a brief built on public and EFRU data, the reinsurer thesis is wrong.

competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Hygiene Technologies International (HygieneTech), Rimkus, Safeguard EnviroGroup (Brad Kovar), EHS Analytical Solutions. White space: Mostly assessment supply and free guidance are crowded, so the raw 'do smoke testing' and 'publish a protocol' layers are not white space. Dozens of CIH-led firms sell $2k-$4k+ assessments and clearance certificates. AIHA, IICRC/RIA/CIRI, Purdue and EFRU already publish free or cheap protocols. Safeguard EnviroGroup is already pitching a 'defensible framework' to carriers. State agencies (AB 1795 drafts) planned to certify IHs, contractors and labs, which undercuts the training-fee line.

Still unserved: (1) Carrier and TPA operations under AB 1795. Nobody offers a claim-level compliance layer with the 30-day inspection clock, an audit-ready sampling plan mapped to zones, chain-of-custody records and an evidence file, sold as software. Carriers are 'technically opposed' but must comply from 1/1/2027, and CAT surge capacity is the pain. (2) Sampling-design defensibility. Research limits: my web-search budget ran out before I could run Crunchbase, YC and TechCrunch-specific queries. The general startup searches (wildfire smoke assessment startup, chain-of-custody kits, technician network) found only wildfire-detection companies (Pano AI, FireScan, FireSafe AI), none in post-fire smoke-damage assessment. Treat 'no funded startup' as probable, not proven. | How this version avoids them: The co-op sells no assessments and writes no protocol, so HygieneTech, Rimkus, Safeguard, EHS, Home BioTesting and Vert-type firms are contributors and users of the percentile report, not rivals. None can build a neutral cross-vendor dataset because each sees only its own clients, and carrier-vendor data is privileged. EFRU holds about 50-80 homes, does not sell, and is a data partner. Purdue's guidance is method we can cite. IICRC and AIHA publish procedures rather than data. Sedgwick and other TPAs hold claim costs but not lab-grade contamination data and sit on the carrier side. The state will need the data in 2028-29 and is a licensee, not a competitor. title: Lender-Required Curtailment Reports for Data Centers
one_liner: An independent, productized report, like a Phase I environmental report but for power, that tells data center lenders how many hours a campus can legally run its generators when the grid curtails it.
customer: Debt originators, underwriters and portfolio managers who finance data centers where the lender carries power risk directly: neocloud GPU-backed delayed-draw loans, spec and powered-land developers without an investment-grade tenant, and ABS/CMBS arrangers and rating analysts. The borrower pays at closing, as it already does for lender-required third-party reports. Independent engineers and lender counsel are the channel. Start with PJM and ERCOT campuses.
problem: Every underwriting model assumes that if PJM or ERCOT curtails the campus, the on-site generators cover it. Federal engine rules and state air permits cap those engines at roughly 100 hours a year, with at most 50 for non-emergency use, and none of it can be run for money or under a financial arrangement. Texas SB 6 even states that it does not authorize violating emissions limits. A campus curtailed for 200 hours can be legally uncovered after 100. Lenders have no independent way to check this. The operator's own consultant is conflicted, and independent engineers are generalists. The exposure is real but unquantified, and it will be priced once someone quantifies it.
solution: A standardized 'Curtailment Runway Report', delivered in about five business days. It has four parts. (1) The permit-derived legal runway: per-engine hour caps, engine tier, allowed uses, monitoring and reporting duties, and remaining headroom. (2) Operational runway: fuel on site, paralleling and telemetry status, and the test and maintenance hours already consumed. (3) A curtailment-exposure distribution for the campus's utility and market zone. (4) A cost-to-cure estimate (permit modification, SCR, hour cap changes). Every report cites the permit conditions it relies on and is reviewed by a retained air attorney. A portfolio subscription adds permit-change alerts and annual surveillance refreshes. Campuses that score badly become inbound leads for the sharpened dual-mode permit service.
why_now: PJM's July 2026 auction was 6.8 GW short and its board plan lets large loads bring their own capacity or accept earlier curtailment. The curtailment rules are now credit terms rather than a policy debate. Texas SB 6 requires 75 MW+ loads to disclose backup generation and lets ERCOT direct deployment, so disclosure data will exist for the first time. Data center financing volume is large and recurring, and power availability is now the top diligence item. LLM-assisted structuring of permit PDFs collapses the cost of producing a first-draft report, while attorney review keeps it defensible.
revenue_model: $20-45k per closing report, paid by the borrower through the lender's third-party report budget. Annual surveillance refresh at $8-12k per campus. Lender or rating-agency portfolio subscriptions at $150-400k a year for unlimited reports and change alerts. Illustrative sizing to validate: 150 financings a year x $30k, plus 400 refreshes x $8k, plus 10 subscriptions x $250k, is roughly $10M annual revenue. Gross margin is high once permits are structured, because the same permit dataset serves every report. A white-label channel to independent engineers is a second line.
non_obvious_insight: The parent's permit dataset is worth more as a warning than as an unlock. Everyone else asks how much diesel can become capacity. The same facts show that the fallback everyone already assumes is often illegal past the cap, which is a downside risk with a faster buyer and no retrofit capex. Lenders reliably pay for independent third-party reports that gate a closing (Phase I environmental reports are the analogy, and the database company behind them proved the data business). Independence is the product. The operator's consultant cannot sell the same report, and aggregators profit from enrollment and have no incentive to say 'no'. A bad score also creates the demand the unlock business could never verify.

title: Hall-Ready Gate for Liquid-Cooled GPU Tranches
one_liner: A fixed-price, 10-business-day release/hold decision, made 60-90 days before GPU delivery, on whether a liquid-cooled data hall will be energized and flowing when the racks arrive.

problem: In a delayed-draw GPU facility, the lender funds a GPU purchase order on the sponsor's word that the hall will be ready. IEs certify construction draws. The technical advisors seen in GPU deals check fleet files, telemetry and power documents (per Peony). The RFS date is a sponsor sales number. NVL72-class racks have no air-cooled fallback, so the loop must be proven flushed, filled and leak-tested before any tray draws power. That work is done last, by scarce people. The parent's weakness was a broad 'better IE' pitch, sold through trust-gated relationships, with no software moat and an unproven right of site access. All of these are addressed below.
solution: One product for one decision, the 'Gate Memo'. It is $30K fixed, delivered in 10 business days. That keeps liability small and stops us from being an IE substitute. Access is solved with a free 'Readiness Rider', a two-page information-covenant and hold-point rider that finance counsel can paste into GPU facility documents. It gives the lender the evidence pack and one site visit as a condition precedent to each GPU tranche. The rider is both the access mechanism and the lead generator. After the gate, a $6K/month watch runs until RFS.

That is pulling in mid-market credit funds that copy the structure without an infrastructure bench. Liquid-cooled racks removed the air-cooled fallback. Liquid-cooling engineers top a Q2 2026 US bottleneck index (Spencer Ogden, scarcity 80/100), and one missing controls technician can hold a finished hall out of service. Lenders are capping neocloud exposure and neocloud deals are stalling on credit risk. Satellite vendors have commoditized the exterior view, so the interior last 90 days is the scarce truth.
revenue_model: $30K per Gate Memo and $6K/month per hall for the watch. A retainer of $75K per fund buys 3 gates. title: Consent Ledger for Land-Scheme Family Cohorts
one_liner: A cohort-priced heir-consent ledger sold to the family 'treasurer' of heirs from ONE 1960s-80s land-buying company or settlement scheme, with a partner law firm as the legal entity of record and a recurring Title Watch on top.
customer: The 'family treasurer': the salaried eldest or most solvent sibling (30-55, in Nairobi, Nakuru, Dallas or Dubai) of a family whose parent or grandparent was an allottee or member of one named land-buying company or settlement scheme in one county (pick one scheme in Murang'a, Kiambu, Nakuru or Trans Nzoia through the founder's own church/alumni/clan network). Distribution partners are the scheme's officials and welfare committee. One partner law firm is the entity of record for all legal work.
problem: Judges flagged three flaws in the parent: thin unit economics (field trips per single estate eat the KES 15-25k fee), the Advocates Act risk of a non-lawyer company selling a 'court-ready bundle' (from memory, unverified), and unproven diaspora willingness to pay. The underlying pain is real but narrower than 'succession': the blocker is proving that all 8-20 heirs were found, asked and agreed, and getting them to sign at all. There is also a sharper trigger than paperwork guilt: land in a dead man's name is an easy target for forged transfers and brokers, and absent children fear waking up to find it sold. A generic 'succession kit' has neither the density to be profitable nor a legal shape that survives scrutiny.
solution: Three steps, each cheap to buy. (0) 'Title Check', KES 1,500 over WhatsApp: photo of the title or parcel number, official search (about KES 500 fee, verify), LLM read of the result, one-page plain-language answer: registered owner, is that person dead, who must be involved. (1) 'Consent Ledger', KES 18k (KES 14k cohort price when 8+ estates from the same chief's location are booked): Kenyan name-variant-reconciled heir map, list of required consents, and a live status board the treasurer shares in the family WhatsApp group ('9 of 14 heirs signed, 3 outstanding, reasons'). A home-area agent runs one scheduled 'signing day' per chief's location per month for chief's-letter requests, ID copies, thumbprints and video consent; heirs elsewhere sign by ID-video on WhatsApp witnessed by the nearest agent. Output is a non-legal 'Consent and Kinship Evidence Pack' with a dispute flag (silent heir, second household, contested claim). The partner law firm receives the pack through a case-management seat, drafts, files and shepherds the case, and bills its own scale fee directly; the company never drafts affidavits or quotes legal fees. (2) 'Title Watch', KES 4k per parcel per year: alerts on registry changes plus a caution/restriction workflow run through the advocate. Asset discovery (SACCO, coop, UFAA letters) is a flat add-on sold only after grant, since UFAA beneficiary claims need the confirmed grant first.
why_now: LLMs now read scanned titles, IDs and share certificates and reconcile Kenyan name variants for cents a page, and drafting copilots (Wakili-Intel appeared July 2026 as a hobby project) are commoditising the paperwork, so the scarce, defensible piece moves to field evidence and multi-heir consent, which is still custom work. The settlement-scheme allottee generation is dying now. WhatsApp Business plus M-Pesa/card make small cross-border payments routine, and digitised searches (Ardhisasa; coverage to be verified) cut registry running. None of this worked in 2019: reading messy scans and chatting in Swahili and English at this cost did not exist.
revenue_model: Ladder per estate: KES 1.5k Title Check, then KES 18k ledger (14k at cohort density), then KES 3k flat advocate seat fee per file (software and case management charge, explicitly not a fee split; verify with counsel), then KES 4k/yr Title Watch, then KES 5k asset-discovery add-on after grant. Assumption to test: at cohort density, field plus search plus ops cost is about KES 7-8k per ledger versus KES 12-15k for one-off estates, giving roughly 45-55% gross margin and about KES 26-30k first-year revenue per estate. A county team (coordinator, 2 agents, share of ops, about KES 3M a year) breaks even near 200 estates a year, which one large scheme can supply. Title Watch gives recurring revenue that the parent lacked.

Neighbouring estates in one scheme share the same registry, chief, original allottee list, surnames and often the same feuds, so every ledger makes the next one cheaper and better (name-variant dictionary, known-disputer flags, chief relationships). That density economy is invisible to per-estate advocates and to national software. Third, fear of land-grabbing is the purchase trigger, so sell 'protect it' first and 'sort the succession' second.

Core metrics: days from intake to all heirs signed, percent of heirs signed on the first visit, and check-to-ledger conversion. Kill test: fewer than 3 of 40 checkers buy a ledger.

title: Keep-the-Amps: Electrical Carve-Out for Plant Liquidations
one_liner: A 3,000-dollar electrician-verified 'in-place value memo' sold to industrial liquidators, trustees' counsel and corporate closure teams, so the switchgear and transformers are carved out of the equipment auction and sold with the real estate as a powered shell.
customer: Wedge: the 15-30 mid-size Midwest industrial liquidation auctioneers, and the panel trustees, receivers' counsel and corporate-real-estate disposition managers who hire them when a plant with at least 2 MW of service goes dark in OH, PA, MI or IN. Not manufacturers, not brokers.
problem: A plant liquidation has two teams that never talk. The equipment auctioneer sells presses, CNCs and often the switchgear, bus duct and transformers as used-equipment or scrap lots. The real-estate side lists square feet and dock doors. The energized service is the scarce asset (large transformers run about 128 weeks, switchgear 44-90+ weeks, so a buyer who has to replace them loses a year or more), and it is destroyed or stripped in the gap between the two teams. The trustee or seller has a fiduciary or financial duty to maximise proceeds but no document showing what the gear is worth in place versus removed. A secured mortgage lender and an equipment lender may also be fighting over what is a fixture.
solution: Sell one fixed-scope deliverable, the 'Powered-Shell Memo', in 8 days: (1) licensed electrician's one-day walk-through with one-line diagram, nameplates, gear age, thermography and spare capacity; (2) a carve-out schedule marking every item of electrical infrastructure as 'stays with the building' or 'safe to sell', with in-place value (replacement cost plus lead-time cost) against scrap and used-lot value; (3) utility service status (energized, disconnected, minimum-bill exposure) and a one-line check of air and wastewater permit status (shutdown, fees current, notification-only transfer), demoted to a checkbox because Ohio EPA transfer is easy; (4) a buyer-agnostic data-room cut that a data-center, battery, cold-storage or manufacturing buyer can underwrite. The fee is a flat cost line in the auction budget, paid from proceeds at closing, so the estate needs no upfront cash.
why_now: Buyers are paying for existing energized shells (TeraWulf/Anthropic's $19B lease on a shuttered aluminum plant, the former Goodyear plant in Akron running about 150 MW), and transformer and switchgear lead times are still measured in years. Plant closures and manufacturer distress continue in 2026, so supply of dead plants is steady. Before the AI-power scramble a stripped switchgear lineup was worth scrap; now it is worth a year of a buyer's schedule.
revenue_model: $3,000 flat per plant (electrician cost about $1,300, analyst about 4 hours, roughly 55% gross margin), paid at closing or as a budgeted line in the liquidation. Add-ons: $1,200 buyer-ready data-room cut, $9,000 for multi-plant corporate closures (3-5 sites), and a $6k-$12k annual retainer for auctioneers who want a standing right to use the memo in their pitches. No percentage of sale price and no brokerage, which avoids the licence problem and the conflict the parent's success fee had. Later: license the anonymised gear-and-value dataset. Bottom-up: 150 to 250 qualifying Midwest industrial disposals a year at $3k-$4k is about $0.5M-$1M of report revenue for one small team before retainers, which is enough to fund the next two offspring-style expansions, not a venture-scale market by itself.
non_obvious_insight: The thing that destroys the power asset in a dead plant is the equipment auction itself, not neglect. The liquidator is paid to turn gear into cash quickly, the real-estate broker never sees the gear list, and nobody owns the question 'is the switchgear worth more bolted to the building?'. The memo is not a report on the building, it is a decision document that changes what goes in the auction catalogue, and it gives the trustee defensible cover for keeping it out.

title: Bench-Truth Diligence for Biotech Investors
one_liner: Sell seed VCs, pharma BD teams and AI-bio founders confidential 'does this paper's key result actually work?' intelligence, from anonymous postdoc consensus polls up to paid replication of the one key experiment.
customer: Seed and Series A biotech VCs, corporate venture arms, pharma BD and scouting teams evaluating academic spinouts or in-licensing, and AI-bio startups building on published wet-lab claims. Pay $4-6k for a poll-only memo and $15-40k for a key-experiment replication.
problem: Investors and BD teams can't tell which high-profile papers replicate. The truth exists as hallway consensus: 'that result only works in the first author's hands', 'nobody outside that lab can get the organoid protocol to run', 'cells were cultured as previously described' with four layers of citations. Formal diligence hires KOL consultants who are conflicted and often the PI's friends, or a CRO that needs 4 months and a full protocol. Bad academic-asset bets burn $5-20M before anyone notices.
solution: Wedge product 'Bench Pulse': in 5 business days, poll 8-15 vetted, paid, anonymous postdocs and senior techs working in the exact subfield about the named claim, reagents and protocol. Deliver a structured memo with consensus, red flags, the Figure-3 problem, which reagents or lots are fragile, and a 'what to test first' plan. Upsell: 'Key-Figure Replication'. A pool of laid-off or between-position scientists runs the single decisive experiment in 3-4 weeks in rented bench space (not on university property), with pre-registered success criteria and blinded readout.
why_now: Biotech funding since 2023 rewards capital efficiency, so seed funds want cheaper, faster kill decisions. Pharma is shopping for early assets in academia and abroad. AI-bio companies are building on published wet-lab claims with little bench sense. NIH disruption and biotech layoffs have released a large pool of very good bench scientists who want paid, flexible work. Expert-network compliance norms are now well understood, so a compliant structure is feasible.
revenue_model: Fixed-fee per poll memo and per replication study. Annual retainer for funds that want a pipeline-wide 'bench pulse' (about $30-60k). Optional success-fee or advisory equity for AI-bio startups.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not lab capacity, it is candid consensus. Replication is expensive, but the postdoc informal network already knows which labs' results hold up. The winning move is to monetize that gossip compliantly and only spend on replication after the poll narrows the question. GLG-style expert calls fail because they interview one conflicted senior person instead of 10 juniors who actually do the pipetting.

Build the compliant NDA plus anonymity protocol with a lawyer for about $3k. Offer 3 seed funds a free poll on one asset they are already looking at. Convert the fund that reacts to a paid $5k poll, then upsell one replication. Pay panelists $150-300 per poll from the first revenue.

- GLG or Guidepoint can copy the poll cheaply once it is proven, since they already sell surveys.
- Anonymity is leaky in subfields of 20-50 people.
- Postdocs risk their careers and may breach university confidentiality or employment terms.
- A negative poll about a named PI's paper carries defamation and tortious-interference exposure.
- A replication that fails in a new lab does not prove the claim is false, which is the ambiguity buyers hate.

title: AI Chat-History Exposure Assessments for Breach Counsel
one_liner: When infostealers grab employees' AI sessions, tell breach counsel what the attacker could actually have read and whether notification is triggered.
customer: Incident-response boutiques, privacy and breach law firms, cyber-insurer panel vendors, and enterprise DPOs. Priced per incident.
problem: Infostealer logs exposed AI sessions tied to 80,000+ corporate domains, and 358 of 482 large companies analyzed had stolen ChatGPT/OpenAI sessions. A stolen session is a searchable archive of contracts, source code, and personal data, and it bypasses MFA. IR tooling was built for mailboxes and file shares, so nobody can say whether an AI-history breach triggers legal notification.
solution: Ingest infostealer-feed hits mapped to employee AI accounts. Combine them with the customer's enterprise export or compliance-API data to classify the sampled chats after the theft window by data class (PII, PHI, credentials, deal information, source code). Deliver a notification-decision memo, an affected-person list, remediation steps (session revocation, key rotation), and an insurer-ready timeline.
why_now: The 2026 infostealer data shows stolen AI sessions at scale. Enterprise AI adoption now puts sensitive work in chat, and insurers are adding AI exclusions, so they want scoping evidence before paying.
revenue_model: $5-25K per incident, with $1-2K per month monitoring retainers and channel referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: The breach is not the stolen cookie but the content behind it, and notification law turns on data, not credentials. No tool in the IR stack handles AI transcripts, so a small team can own the category before platform vendors bother.
first_30_days: Sign 3 IR boutiques as channel partners. Build a classification pipeline over enterprise chat exports. Run the first paid assessments at a $7.5K flat fee using hits from commercial infostealer-intel feeds.
lineage: original (tournament survivor)
competition_context:
Competitor check: GAP. Closest players: Hudson Rock (Cavalier, infostealers.com, CavalierGPT), SpyCloud, Flare, Constella Intelligence. White space: Across the pages I could fetch, no vendor sells the specific deliverable: a counsel-facing 'what could the attacker have read, and does notification trigger' determination for a stolen AI session. The gap sits between three groups. Infostealer-intel vendors (Hudson Rock, SpyCloud, Flare, Constella) detect the stolen session but stop there. AI-DLP and DSPM vendors (Varonis, Cyera, Harmonic, Cyberhaven, Reco, Purview) classify current or real-time chat data for the customer's own governance. Breach-review platforms (Relativity and IR firms) build notification lists but show no ingestion of AI chat transcripts. What remains open is the forensic and legal bridge: joining the theft window from the feed with provider-side session-access evidence and the chat content, then producing a privilege-friendly memo and affected-person list.

Caveats on the wedge:
- The WebSearch budget ran out, so I could not check funded startups, Product Hunt, YC or open-source projects. A stealth startup is possible.
- I could not verify the '358 of 482' or '80,000 domains' figures.
- The wedge depends on data access. A theft of a personal or free-tier account leaves the employer with no export. Only Enterprise and Edu tenants have admin export or Compliance API data, and I could not confirm the current API terms because the OpenAI help pages returned 403.
- A stolen cookie in a feed does not prove the attacker viewed the chats, so the assessment depends on provider audit logs that only OpenAI or the tenant admin can see.
- Any vendor holding the customer's chat data (Cyera, Varonis, Purview) can add this as a services line quickly.
